speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house I should like to make a statement with regard to the international situation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Has the Prime Minister leave to proceed with the statement?

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
As I said in the house on Saturday, the United Nations security council failed at its last meeting to adopt any of the three resolutions which were before it concerning the situation in Lebanon and Jordan. The Secretary of State for External Affairs returned to Ottawa on Saturday evening and over the week end he reported on his discussions with the British foreign secretary, Mr. Selwyn Lloyd; the Secretary of State of the United States, Mr. Dulles; Mr. Ham-marskjold and others.
I know that members of the house will appreciate the fact that it would not be fitting or helpful at this very anxious time to disclose the views expressed in those discussions. I should add, relative to the answer I gave on Saturday last to a question asked by the Leader of the Opposition, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs made known in his discussions the opinion of the Canadian government that no military activity should be undertaken by any nation in any place beyond Jordan and Lebanon.
In addition, the week end has witnessed the publication of a Soviet proposal on the Middle East, namely a proposal for a meeting of the heads of government of the United States, the United Kingdom, France, India and the U.S.S.R., with the participation of the Secretary General of the United Nations. This initiative came against the background of Soviet and Bulgarian troop manoeuvres on their southern borders.
I need hardly tell the house that, the situation having already reached critical proportions, such a proposal is bound to have a considerable impact on the thinking of people everywhere.
Much of the language in which the Soviet invitation is couched is so provocative in tone that it tends to add yet another complicating
factor at an already very serious moment in world affairs by tempting the rejection of the invitation on the ground of its not being genuine. Tensions have, however, reached such a stage that every opportunity should be explored to discuss the causes of tension in the interests of heading off the possibility of war.
President Eisenhower has said more than once that he is ready to meet with the Soviet leaders if a meeting would contribute to the cause of peace. As I stated in this house last November, I still believe that no nation should or dare shut the door on any matter that offers the prospect of any solution or even a diminution of international tensions. In view of the recent developments in the Middle East I believe that the problem of that region should be discussed at the highest level, and that such talks should be held as soon as possible because of the present perilous situation, the urgency of which has been so greatly intensified by the developments of the last few days.
In this very explosive situation, in the interests of assuring that the international temperature be not increased, the Canadian government would expect that the status quo be maintained in the region of the Middle East, and would welcome from all the countries concerned assurances such as those which were given by Prime Minister Macmillan in respect of Iraq in the House of Commons at Westminster on July 17, in particular that all members of NATO will exercise the greatest caution in national action which might involve the alliance as a whole. In the meantime we should all continue to co-operate in the discussions now being carried on at the United Nations, having as their objective the solution of those problems of which the United Nations is now completely seized.
The council meets again today to consider a compromise Japanese proposal on Lebanon, and for the purpose of the record I think I should refer to that motion, which is as follows:
1.	The security council, having heard the charges of the representative of Lebanon concerning the interference of the U.A.R. in the internal affairs of Lebanon and the reply of the U.A.R., invites the UNOGIL to continue to develop its activities pursuant to the security council resolution of June 11, 1958;
2.	Requests the secretary general to make arrangements forthwith for such measures in addition to those envisaged in the resolution of June 11, 1958, as he may consider necessary in the light of the

External Affairs-Middle East present crisis with a view to enabling the United Nations to fulfil the general purposes established in that resolution and which will, in accordance with the charter, serve to ensure the territorial integrity and political independence of Lebanon so as to make possible the withdrawal of U.S. forces from Lebanon;
3.	Requests the secretary general to report to the security council on the arrangements made;
4.	Calls upon the governments concerned to co-operate fully in the implementation of this resolution.
I think Canadians will all agree that during the last few days the Secretary of State for External Affairs, both in Washington and New York, has earned for this country the tribute of representatives of other countries as a result of the skill and ability he has shown during the discussions in both those cities.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
After discussing the whole situation with him at great length yesterday I suggested that, while he has responsibilities in the house, it might be well for him to go to New York to take personal charge of the Canadian delegation during the debate before the security council.
With regard to the present I would like to go further than I am able to go, but I would like to tell the house and the country that this government, I feel with the approval of the Canadian people as a whole, is doing everything it possibly can to bring about an agreement between the nations of the free world whereby constructive action may be taken promptly. I do not want to overemphasize the gravity of the situation, but at the same time I do not want to understate it. For that reason I want the house and the country to know that there are no hours today in so far as the Secretary of State for External Affairs, myself and other members of the cabinet are concerned. We are trying to do our part, as a country which has no direct interest, to bring about a solution which is reasonable, in accordance with the principles laid down in the United Nations charter and within the ambit of that charter.
Over the week end I personally addressed urgent messages to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, to the Prime Minister of India and to President Eisenhower, suggesting that there be a positive and immediate response to the Khrushchev message. The suggestions made are now being considered in the various capitals as well as, I hope, in the NATO council in New York.
It would be less than proper to spell out those suggestions, but I can say this: that in the light of what I said earlier we believe that a meeting is necessary at top level, and I feel, too, that the United Nations security council in session offers possibilities on which I will not elaborate at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will have heard with great interest and, I think, understanding, the statement of the Prime Minister on a situation which in the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs *-and I do not think it was an overstatement-is grave, though not, as he put it, critical.
I can speak only for hon. members of my own party, but we certainly hope to give the Prime Minister, the government and particularly the Secretary of State for External Affairs, full support in all the efforts they are making for peace and stability in the Middle East on behalf of a country which is a member of the United Nations, because as signatories to the United Nations charter we have all of us obligations for furthering peace and stability in the world.
I can appreciate the pressure both physical and mental under which the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and their colleagues are working at this time, having had some experience with that kind of pressure myself. I entirely agree with the Prime Minister in the statement he has made and the suggestion, which I understand the government has made to other governments perhaps even more directly concerned, that no action should be taken by the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States in present circumstances beyond the borders of Lebanon and Jordan; that they should do what they can to discourage action of that kind from any other quarter, and that they should lend their weight to any policy which would establish the status quo for the time being in this area.
A new development occurred over the week end in the invitation by the head of the Soviet government to the governments of the United Kingdom, the United States, France and India for a summit conference to deal with this particular matter and, as I understand it, to deal only with this particular matter. We have heard at this time with satisfaction that the Prime Minister has already indicated to three of these governments that, in the view of the Canadian government, they should adopt a positive approach to this invitation. He did not mention whether he had sent a message of the kind which he had suggested to London, Washington and New Delhi, to Paris as well, but I assume that has also been done.
In common with other hon. members of parliament I have been asked questions on this subject, and in reply to some of those questions I have said that in my own view

I think it would be most unwise for the three western powers to take a negative stand on Mr. Khrushchev's invitation to a conference. I added that I hoped the Canadian government was urging them not to give this invitation an unqualified refusal, and therefore I heard with pleasure, as I am sure other hon. members heard with pleasure, of the stand taken by the government.
There remains the question of how this invitation can be most effectively dealt with if it is not to be given an unqualified refusal. The Prime Minister was good enough this morning to give me some confidential information on developments, and I appreciate that very much. I indicated to him at that time that I hoped to be in a position this afternoon to ask him a question on this matter, and I confess that in that question I would have expressed my own view as to how this invitation might be dealt with. There will be no opportunity for such a question because orders of the day will not be reached, but perhaps because the Prime Minister has quite rightly brought up the matter I might indicate my own view as to how this particular matter could be treated in the present circumstances and at the present time, as it has to be dealt with quickly.
In view of the Soviet government's invitation for an immediate summit conference on the Middle East crisis, and in view of the reports we have observed in the press that the United Kingdom and United States governments might not find it possible to accept this invitation in the form in which it was extended-and I can certainly understand that in view of the language of the invitation -but in view also of the desirability of not turning down this invitation in any unconditional way, would it not be desirable for the Canadian member at the security council which is meeting at this moment to make a proposal to the effect that the security council should appoint a subcommittee of representatives of the United Kingdom, United States, France and the Soviet union, and by special invitation India, under the chairmanship of the Secretary General of the United Nations to consider ways and means of resolving the current Middle East crisis? This subcommittee could meet, and I hope would meet, immediately at a place to be determined by its chairman, the secretary general, and it could be suggested that the countries appointed to it be represented by their heads of government. That would ensure that the meeting in question would be at the top level of governmental representation, and it would also ensure that the meeting in question would be held under the auspices of the
External Affairs-Middle East United Nations and indeed under the chairmanship of the Secretary General of the United Nations.
In putting forward this proposal, Mr. Speaker, I realize that the Prime Minister has a great deal of information available to him which is not available to everyone, and he may have considerations in mind and there may be factors he knows about that bear on this proposal. But I should like to put it forward to him for the consideration of the government and possibly for consideration at the United Nations security council, in the hope that this might be a way of dealing with the invitation which would underline that our approach to these matters in the west is not negative, and which indeed might have some kind of constructive result which would assist in removing the shadow of fear and war that hangs over the world at the moment.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group are glad to note that the government is opposed to extending the political bonanza handed the Soviet union by certain actions taken outside the United Nations. We are also glad to hear of the government's support for summit talks, and the Prime Minister's request for an immediate and positive response to the Khrushchev invitation to those summit talks. We go right along with him; we think it is a most constructive approach to this most serious situation.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of this group I want to express our opposition to unilateral action and our continued support of work toward United Nations mediation. Our sincere hope is that mediation will soon result, in the near days ahead, in the announcement by the governments of Great Britain and the United States that they have withdrawn their troops from Lebanon and Jordan.

maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I do want to thank the Leader of the Opposition for the unity displayed at this very important phase of international difficulties. I welcome, and this government welcomes, any suggestions that come from him because of his experience, from which none of us will try at any time to detract.
This is a time when we must act positively. This is no time for stagnant thinking based on forms that may have been applicable in the past. It is equally no time for side issues and the making of generalizations that cannot have any effect other than not contributing to a solution of an immediate problem.

Proposed Legislation
The proposal made by the Leader of the Opposition is-and I do not want to spell out, as I said a while ago, the representations made in the personal messages I referred to earlier-very close to a suggestion I made and suggestions that are in mind and are now under consideration. I can assure not only the hon. gentleman but members of the house that every constructive proposal that any hon. member has to offer will be given the most careful and continuing examination.
There is a strength in our democracy and our parliamentary system, and that strength is that in times of difficulty we do not allow partisanship to separate us. We may have differing opinions on the means but never on the objectives. Again I emphasize the assurance that at this time, when a community of counsel is so necessary, the expression of viewpoints by hon. gentlemen will at all times receive the most complete examination, and out of a variety of suggestions one can often bring forth the epitome that will bring about a solution. I shall go no further than that at this time, but again I thank the house for the courtesy shown in making possible this short explanation this afternoon.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES

speakeroldname: Mr. G. J. Mcllrailh (Ottawa West) moved:
maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of establishing free trade between Canada and the Federation of the West Indies.
He said: In rising to present this motion for the approval of the house Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but feel that it is in some respects most appropriate that it should come forward for discussion today, because we have just concluded three days of discussion in committee of the whole on the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. In addition, we just this morning had the honour of having before us in an unofficial way in this chamber the Prime Minister of the new member of the commonwealth, Ghana. I feel, therefore, it is appropriate in the light of those circumstances that this motion should come forward for debate, and I hope approval, today.
It will be seen from the order paper that this is the second appointed Monday for the discussion of private members' motions. I hope that at the conclusion of this day hon. members will feel that the discussion of this motion has been such as to be indicative of the real worth of private members' days, and that they will feel this is a useful contribution and a very proper use of that right of private members to bring matters before this house for debate.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I must confess to some difficulty in wording the motion. My concern is with the subject of trade, increasing our trade with the West Indies, but I wanted to get the motion forward in a way that would result not in a mere academic discussion of free trade, but rather in an effort to free trade to the greatest possible extent with this particular area. When I say "free trade to the greatest possible extent", I refer to not only matters like the customs tariff, which seems to be the traditional thing to discuss, but the matter of currency exchange restrictions, shipping and all the other restrictions that may be imposed on the exchange of goods between two countries.
At the outset of my remarks I might also express my own appreciation to the Minister of Trade and Commerce for having given this subject the attention he did in his remarks during the consideration of the estimates of trade and commerce. I was greatly pleased
Canada

West Indies Trade to hear him recognize the importance of the subject and deal with it in full recognition of that importance.
There is such a great abundance of material written about this subject within this last year or two that it seems difficult tc narrow it down to what to present to the house in the space of 40 minutes. Perhaps it is well for us to be specific and recognize that in our statistics on trade it is difficult to separate the trade figures of the Federation of the West Indies from the figures of the British Caribbean area. It is well if we recall to our minds that the federation about which I wish to speak includes specifically Jamaica, Trinidad, Barbados, the Leeward islands and the Windward Islands but excludes British Honduras, British Guiana and the Bahamas of the British Caribbean group.
It is well also to recall that the federated area is really responsible for approximately -and this is only a rough approximation- three quarters of our trade with the whole area. It is well also to recall that their constitution came into effect only on January 3 of this year and that they held their federal election on March 25 of this year. I think some hon. members will not find it difficult to recall that date because of its close proximity to a certain other event which took place in Canada a few days later. Then there was the inauguration of the federal legislature on April 22, 1958. I am sure the government indicated the significance they attached to that event by the team which they sent to represent Canada on that occasion.
In dealing with the subject in a more specific way, it can be said at once to me, if the motion is read in a strict and narrow way: Oh, you do not recognize the fact that the federation does not have legislative control over its foreign trade; they do not yet have a customs union. That is perfectly true, Mr. Speaker. The federation does not yet have a customs union, though there seems to be every indication that they are moving toward it. In any event a commission is examining that subject at the present time, and the best information I can get is that the report of that commission will be available within a matter of a few weeks or months, much in advance of the time that it was expected to be ready when the commission was set up.
It could also be said, on a narrow reading of the motion: Oh, you cannot deal with free trade between Canada and the Federation of the West Indies because they do not have control of their own foreign exchange. I am quite aware of that fact. I am aware of the fact that the United Kingdom still has control of the foreign exchange for the area, but I respectfully submit that that is only

Canada-West Indies Trade one more reason why we should be discussing this matter and examining it rather than withholding discussion of it.
The trade figures are rather interesting. The Minister of Trade and Commerce in his remarks indicated the importance of the trade of that area and I do not intend to elaborate very much on that point; but it is interesting to note that in 1936 our exports to the West Indies federated area amounted to $8,629,000 and our imports to some $13,305,000. In 1957 they had risen so that our commodity exports to that area amounted to $40,276,000 in value and our commodity imports amounted to some $58,430,000 in value. Of course, in addition there are other factors that would enter into an exchange of currency or balance of payments like the vast tourist business in the area from Canada and things like the presence of West Indies students in our universities in Canada.
Those figures will illustrate the importance of the trade in that area. But more particularly the products involved serve to indicate its importance to Canada, imports, as I assess the order of dollar importance, were sugar, bauxite and alumina, petroleum, molasses, rum, cocoa, coffee, spices and citrus fruits. Our exports were wheat flour, fish, textiles and manufactures, meat, tobacco, lumber, motor vehicles, milk, mixed feeds, boots and shoes, potatoes and a variety of manufactured articles.
From these products and the nature of the commodities exchanged it will be seen that the area is, I venture to suggest, complementary with respect to those products; that is, the products it has for export to us are as complementary to the products we have for export to that area as are those of any other area in the world. I do not know of any better example one could get of two areas where the commodities sought to be exchanged are more complementary to each other than are those of this area of the Federation of the West Indies and Canada.
That situation, of course, is easy to understand when one recalls the great differences in climate. It seems to me that this whole area is one in which we should naturally have a high interest for many reasons, among others the fact that for some 200 years now we have shared the same association with the British empire, now known as the commonwealth or the commonwealth and its antecedent form, whatever the terminology was, depending on what date you were talking about. This historical association has gone on in common between us for the order of 200 years, which is quite a long time in our history.
There is the naturally complementary nature of their production and our production.

Then there is this new matter we have in common, namely the gradual enlargement of their control of their own political destiny as indicated by the federation this year. Anyone who has regard to the development of political freedom within Canada and our own history in that respect I think must share a feeling of rejoicing and good will that the West Indies have now come together in their federation, in somewhat different form than we but none the less a distinctive step in their development and evolution.
Now I wish to deal with the trade itself. It is interesting that in this relatively small area which I consider to be of great importance we maintain at the present time two trade commissioners, one in Jamaica and one in Trinidad. It is also interesting that we have seen fit to take part in organizing two trade fairs, somewhat new in form, to take place in these two parts of the federation. These trade fairs of 1959 are rather significant, because so far as I know they are developing along a somewhat new pattern for Canada in that they are in the nature of joint enterprises between Canadian business and the government. I think the minister would agree with that description.
I have spoken about trade and I am aware of the usual difficulties with respect to this subject, but it seems to me there are some aspects of it which we could and should usefully discuss in this house. One of the suggestions I am going to make is with respect to the matter of substantially enlarging our activities in respect of trade in spite of the difficulties involved. There are two views abroad, one that there is a little too much optimism and the other that there is not sufficient optimism with regard to trade possibilities, but I believe with the optimists that a great deal can be done to enlarge our trade. I believe this involves imaginative and constructive steps on the part of the government, and that imaginative and constructive suggestions in this house are required in order to achieve this end.
In any discussion of a general nature in this house it is difficult to deal with the matter in detail, commodity by commodity, and I have been avoiding doing so because I think the proper way for the details to be dealt with is by the working groups in the Department of Trade and Commerce, who are thoroughly competent and have all the data readily available for that kind of consideration which is conducive to the best results. I believe, furthermore, that our function here is to indicate the political objective, and that what we are seeking to do is to set

up the machinery so that the details can be worked out by the departmental officials.
There are one or two particular matters which I would like to mention at this time. We could make a useful contribution to the enlargement of this trade by organizing and marshalling studies on the whole question of grading and presenting products of the federation to be sold in this country. It seems to me that they produce a large number of items which we do not have and which we require, and that these items could be presented to this country as exports which would be of benefit not only to the West Indies but to Canada.
I am quite prepared to admit that we have not been able to create a system of grading and handling such items as those requiring refrigeration, packaging and so on, and that this facet of trade must be studied. I believe, however, that one activity which could be undertaken by this government is a study, primarily through its own personnel but which would rapidly be supported by the traders of Canada, with a view to offering assistance to the federation in the methods of standardizing, grading and handling products which could be exported from the West Indies to Canada.
This naturally brings me to another facet of the subject, which is the question of shipping. I am aware that this matter has been discussed on the estimates during the last three days, and I therefore will not extend my remarks on shipping, as I would rather like to do. My purpose is not to be critical of the government with respect to this matter of trade with the West Indies, although I must admit that I am critical of the government with respect to the discontinuance of the Canadian National Steamships service to the West Indies. I expressed myself on this subject at some length on Friday last, and I can only say that in the light of the historical association between Canada and the British Carribean area, in the light of the profitable trade we have had with that area over the years and in the light of the new political development which has taken place in that area, I cannot alter my position from that of the sharpest criticism of the government for having discontinued in such a precipitous way the service to the area in 1957.
Indeed, upon checking into the background of this subject I was interested to note the consideration given to this matter by the former government, and in particular the announcement made to this House of Commons in, I believe, March of 1956 by the then minister of transport that the shipping service would continue for another five years. That was the policy announced which was supported in a rather fine paragraph or two of
Canada-West Indies Trade a speech by the present Minister of National Revenue on this subject in March of 1957 when, as I read his remarks, he spoke very strongly in favour of the service being continued. Only a few months after this, however, the government of which he became a member after the 1957 election abruptly discontinued the service without a proper explanation to the house, and I respectfully submit without a proper consideration of the factors involved.
It is interesting to note that this service had operated at a profit in the year 1956, though I admit there were some problems concerning it, but in 1957 a strike occurred which was a very difficult strike to settle involving a difficult labour problem, and the minister abruptly announced the discontinuance of the service. I have never been aware that a labour situation or a strike made necessary that kind of precipitate action. That was followed by the decision to sell these ships, although I do not know whether or not they are actually sold as yet. The suggestion was put forward by some of us in the opposition that consideration be given to the possibility of giving one of these ships to the federation so that our mutual trade might be continued.
I hold the view that in the light of all this there must of necessity be a note of sharp criticism in my remarks on that respect of the matter having to do with the shipping service to the federation, particularly at this time and particularly in the light of the announcement by the former government that the service would be continued for about five years.
The other matter for consideration is the question of the kind of action which should be taken, and I would respectfully put forward to the house at this time the suggestion that the kind of action we require is action on the political level direct from the government of Canada to the government of the West Indies. That becomes necessary for this reason. On Friday, when the estimates of the department were before the committee of the whole for discussion, I was very critical of the government for not having taken any action to follow up or consider the proposal for free trade put forward at Mont Tremblant last year by the British Chancellor of the Exchequer.
I will not rehash those arguments, but I want to point out today in the context of the resolution now before the house that had that proposal received the kind of consideration from the Canadian government which it was entitled to receive, and had the Canadian government taken appropriate action with respect to it, discussions would have taken

Canada-West Indies Trade place on the subject to find out precisely what was in the mind of the United Kingdom authorities; there would have been an opportunity to put forward what the Canadians had in mind by way of liberalizing or freeing trade in the areas under the control of the United Kingdom, and this would have brought up directly the matter of currency exchange control in the area we are discussing.
I can only suggest that this debate today and the bringing forward of this subject shows in a practical and real way the consequences of the government's failure to give consideration to this new and, one could almost say, startling proposal by the British Chancellor of the Exchequer. Had the government treated this suggestion properly there would already be under way the kind of detailed study which is required with respect to this area of the Federation of the West Indies.
Now, on this question of the exchange and currency difficulties in the area, I wish to recall to the house a short paragraph of a speech made by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) on January 7, 1958. He was discussing the larger matter of trade with this area, and I should like to read a sentence or two of his speech in the house. It will be found on page 2970 of Hansard:
Perhaps it would be worth considering whether we cannot tie that new part of the commonwealth, as it soon will become, more closely economically and financially to our own country, Canada, by exploring the possibility of free trade between the West Indies and Canada, or a freer trade area, and by tying up our two currencies which would encourage trade and transport between us.
It seems to me that approval of the resolution as it is presented to the house would give the government the kind of support it requires and, indeed, more than giving them this support it might incite them to the kind of action which the country requires to get on with discussions with the West Indies so that steps could be taken to increase trade with each of the component parts of the federation, and if and when the federation does have jurisdiction over its own customs regulations, to deal with the federation on that basis and also to go forward now with the United Kingdom in whatever steps may be taken to relax the exchange controls which now govern that area.
It seems to me that because of the political history of the area, its geographical location and other reasons I have mentioned, we require, and are justified in taking, very imaginative and bold steps with regard to this matter, steps going further than perhaps we might be inclined to take with regard to other countries in the world at this time. And the right time to act is now. I do not

know Mr. Speaker, whether one can correctly use the phrase "politically perfect timing", but to the extent to which one can use such a phrase it seems to me that the timing is politically perfect for this to be done in the light of the arguments I have just advanced.
There are a great many publications to which I could make reference, but perhaps I should not be serving a useful purpose in doing so. There is a great deal I could say by way of appreciation of the work done by the former government.

speechtext: Don't forget to tell us that.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Well, I think it is a very proper thing to do when speaking on the subject, for reasons which I will indicate to the hon. member for Huron. There was the agreement in 1898, the 1912 agreement, then the 1920 agreement, and again in 1925 the agreement which was worked out in that year and which came into force in 1927 but which, curiously enough, is properly referred to as the West Indian Trade Agreement Act of 1926. That 1926 trade agreement act is the agreement under which we have operated in connection with this area for all these years. It was in its time a very bold and imaginative act, and it produced very good results both for this country and for the Caribbean area.
I will not elaborate on the details, but we were granted a sharply reduced tariff on our goods going into that area, the actual rates depending on the island concerned, because they varied with the various parts of the area. However, the reduction was of the order of 50 or 75 per cent of the current tariff granted under the British preferential rate. It was a very successful piece of legislation, and I think the hon. member for Huron, if he studies the problem, would agree that it was an excellent agreement; and I do not know how one could discuss this subject adequately without referring to the West Indian Trade Agreement Act of 1926.
I do not propose to extend my remarks further, but I should like to quote two sentences from a speech made by Sir Grantley Adams, the prime minister of the federation, made at Mount Allison University at the 1957 summer institute when the subject under discussion was "Canada and the West Indies federation". It will be found on page 36 of the publication put out by the university. The first sentence I wish to quote is this:
But we are profoundly convinced that our whole future depends on the closest possible relationship with the Dominion of Canada.
Then a little further on he had this to say:
I am not flattering you. I am not saying it because I am addressing a Canadian audience. What I do say is that we consider our future success will lie with the closest possible understanding between the West Indies and Canada.

Mr. Speaker, that seems to me to present to us both a challenge and a promise. It is a promise which I am sure all hon. members on both sides of this chamber without regard to political affiliation will welcome. I can think of speeches made by the hon. member for St. John Albert (Mr. Bell) on this subject in the past which lead me to believe that this proposal would win his support. Far be it from me to speak for him, but I am sure that he and hon. members of this house in all political parties will welcome the promise inherent in those remarks of the prime minister of the federation. It presents a challenge to us, as I said, and it is in connection with that challenge that I wish to relate my remarks today.
I present this motion to the house today as the kind of answer to the challenge that private hon. members of this house in their capacity as private hon. members can give; and I ask that the Prime Minister of Canada accept that challenge and follow up in acceptance of the challenge with the kind of action that only the government has the power and authority to take. That is action to put in motion immediately in a specific way the political and technical measures on the part of the trade officers that will make our response to the challenge become something of which we will be proud. By that action we will have done a great deal to develop trade with the area, I would hope that the action taken by hon. members will be such as to bring pride to the hearts of all Canadians. I hope they will feel that they have taken the proper action with respect to a member state of the commonwealth at this time.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and in conclusion I want to thank all hon. members for the patience and courtesy with which they have listened to my remarks on this important subject today, all too inadequate though they may have been.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with a feeling of great pleasure at being given an opportunity to take part in this discussion on an extremely important matter. I should like to congratulate most heartily the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) for his splendid presentation. Indeed, his presentation was so exhaustive and complete that in fear of being redundant I shall be forced, to an even greater degree than usual, to bring to my remarks the laconic brevity which I have sought to achieve over the years. I congratulate him, too, on the generally non-political tone of his remarks, and I shall also endeavour to follow that pattern. I shall not engage in a detailed
Canada

West Indies Trade discussion of the development of shipping and the merchant marine in Canada lest I fall into the tendency of criticizing the party to which the hon. member belongs for some of its actions and omissions in years not too far past.
I believe the hon. member is quite right in referring to private members' days as one of the great privileges of a democratic parliamentary system, when we function more as members of a national parliament than as adherents of a political party. I noted that the hon. member was so mellow in his broad attitude that he even referred with apparent equanimity to a certain Canadian event in the month of March.
Coming as I do from the maritimes, a region which has long had intimate and highly satisfactory relations with the West Indies, I am particularly happy to have the opportunity of speaking on this subject at this time. Perhaps there is something appropriate in my so doing, in that I am a member from an island province and we are speaking today about our relations with an archipelago, a group of islands. Not only are Prince Edward Islanders and the people of the maritimes interested in this subject, but I believe it is one in which all Canadians are deeply interested.
I am of the opinion that the terms of the resolution before us are so broad that we must consider more than the economic factors. In considering a proposal for free trade with another political entity we must take into consideration a great many political factors. Therefore I intend to be somewhat general and probably historical-I hope never hysterical-in some of the remarks I propose to make.
It is interesting that we now look upon the development of the second British federation on the North American continent. There are many problems involved in a federation. Some of the scholars in the pristine purity of their analysis have declared that Canada is not a federation but a quasi-federation. However, this is not the time for such constitutional hairsplitting. I think it can be said that there is much in common in the development of Canada from 1867 on and the new federation to the south. Indeed, our population was somewhat similar in 1867, about three million. We have perhaps not advanced as much as many of our earlier statesmen had hoped, but we have advanced magnificently.
We look forward to the political advancement of the British West Indies federation and we look forward to welcoming them as a member of the commonwealth. It was my great pleasure to be present at the United

of making use of them will find increasing favour in that area. I refer to one, the potato. In Prince Edward Island we grow the finest potatoes in the world. We have always been interested in the West Indian market. I am glad to see that over the years there has been improvement in our sales to that market we sold $418,000 worth last year. This market-could be improved and I think it should be improved.
Now while I believe that this is the time to think of these things, I have a feeling it would be a bit unrealistic to expect that a customs union would come about immediately. The history of customs unions has generally been that they are rather slow in their evolution. You will recall that after the second world war there were a great many prospects for customs unions amongst countries which had a good deal in common politically and which had a common goal, their own economic betterment. However, they are still a long way from the fruition of their plans for customs unions.
I am not one of those who say that a customs union or free trade area, to be more precise in the terms of the resolution, could not and might not come about between these two parts of North America, so closely bound by tradition. But I do think that no matter how vigorously the government might move in this direction it is not something which can come about quickly. I will agree that we should draw closer to this area. We, the oldest commonwealth member, rejoice in the development on this hemisphere of another potential member of that wonderful association. I believe, too, we can be helpful. I like the idea that was put forward that perhaps we should develop a Caribbean plan somewhat similar to the Colombo Plan. Some steps have been taken in that direction. The United States, too, has given some technical assistance, but it is only the beginning; the West Indians feel it is only the beginning. I believe we should look upon ourselves as just beginning.
But there is something even broader, and that is that our relations with the West Indies will tax, and test in good measure, Canadian political maturity. It took quite a long time for us to recognize our position in the world. For many years we were much involved in penetration of our own frontiers. But then we moved across and took our place in the world, especially in that north Atlantic triangle which has become so much a part of our history. But we are a member and a part of this hemisphere. As a power with world responsibilities, we cannot look only as far south as Washington and only to the western European world. We have a place of leadership here on this part of the globe.

In close union with this great multi-racial community I think we can go forward to give great leadership in this part of the world. I would envisage that some day-and of course this is only my personal opinion and hope-we might take our place along with a fully independent West Indies federation and member of the commonwealth in the Organization of American states often called the Pan-American union and that that would be the full measure of our continental solidarity and brotherhood with this new and very interesting young nation that we now see before our eyes taking its place in this troubled, difficult yet altogether interesting and challenging world.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from a province which basically depends oh exports for its well-being, I am naturally always greatly interested when there is before the house a motion which deals with either the expansion of trade or a policy of extension of free trade. That is the type of motion with which we are dealing at the present time and which was introduced by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith).
I cannot say that I completely agree with all the remarks of the previous speaker. I am inclined to believe that he was a little bit too much on the pessimistic side and could not see advances in the field of trade between the Federation of the West Indies and Canada in as rapid a time as I am certain the sponsor of the motion and I believe is possible. It is not very often when we find a country with which we have had expanding business over the years coming to our country, as has been done in recent weeks and in recent months, telling us that they would like to buy more from us and asking why we do riot do something to assist them in buying more from Canada.
In more than one important publication it has been pointed out in recent weeks that we in this country are not accepting the challenge of the opportunity for greater exports to the Federation of the West Indies. It was only in recent weeks that I was reading an interesting issue of the commercial letter of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. I refer to their issue No. 2 in March of this year. From it I should like to quote two paragraphs. On page 8 we find this:
The problem of overcoming United Kingdom-oriented buying habits in the West Indies and that of maintaining a competitive price position are primarily sales and production considerations. On a long-term basis, however, the situation offers something more of a challenge to Canada, and at the same time provides an opportunity for this country to take a constructive part in building a prosperous economy in the West Indies.
The market for certain Canadian goods in the next few years is promising. The need for fer-
Canada-West Indies Trade tilizers is expected to grow as agriculture develops, and the market for capital goods and for certain manufactured goods should also expand.
In the same commercial letter of the Canadian Bank of Commerce we find this:
The West Indies, in seeking to build an economy which will raise the level of prosperity, will need the friendly co-operation of many other countries. The outstanding needs of the new federation are stability in the markets for its produce, an inflow of investment capital, and some financial and technical assistance. The country that joins in an attempt to supply these needs will, in the long run, confer considerable benefits upon itself, as far-sighted private interests have already realized.
I believe that this commercial letter, which was issued only in March of this year, is pointing out both to the government and to the industries of this country that there is a challenge that our country can meet as put to us by the Federation of the West Indies and that there is at least the indication that we are perhaps not taking full advantage of the opportunities being presented to us.
As a matter of fact, I am most happy at the increase in the export and import trade in the past few years between what is now the Federation of the West Indies and our own country of Canada. I did not make a study of the same years as those mentioned by the two previous speakers but I note that in 1953 Canada had exports to what is now known as the Federation of the West Indies of some $29,578,000 and that only four years later, in 1957, that figure had increased to $40,276,000. On the other side of the picture, in 1953 we imported in the amount of $23,408,000 and four years later, in 1957, we imported $58,430,000 worth of goods.
It is most interesting to make a study of what are the major imports that we receive from the Federation of the West Indies. If we make a study of what are our major imports, we can then come to a rather full realization as to why our fellow citizens in that part of the commonwealth are most anxious that they should do a greater business with Canada and buy more from our country. Just on the basis of 1957 I find that here in this country we took as much as one-third of our requirements in unrefined sugar from the Federation of the West Indies, one-half of our requirements of molasses and syrups and two-thirds of our requirements of bauxite alumina. Of course I suppose the story would not be complete if I did not mention that we also import from the Federation of the West Indies one-third of our rum. Canadian importation of two-thirds of our requirements in bauxite alumina and one third of our requirements in unrefined sugar means a great deal to Jamaica, especially as regards their market for sugar.
We have not, however, taken advantage of their requests and desires. They not only

Canada-West Indies Trade sent over a most powerful delegation this year to see if they could not buy more from Canada, but they pointed out that they have the dollars with which to buy, something which so many countries do not have. They have all the dollars they require.
Why are they so anxious that we should sell more to them? It is, of course, to use the words of the delegation, because they are worried about the situation whereby on six months' notice Canada could cut off the $1 per hundred pounds preferential. The amazing feature of the trade situation is that Canada gives the Federation of the West Indies $1 preferential per hundred pounds on our imports of unrefined sugar, while the United States gives no preferential whatsoever. Yet in the past the majority of imports which have been going into the Federation of the West Indies have been from the United States and not from Canada. In a one-year period when there was a differential of $3.8 million in Canada there was a differential of $53 million in the United States, so I think we can all very easily realize the fears felt by the people of the federation lest Canada should ever decide to change its mind with respect to the differential. I would like to read very briefly from a most interesting article in the Financial Post of January 18, 1958, written by a Mr. Robert W. McRae, headed "Jamaica's Trade Slogan 'If You've Got It, We'll Buy It' ". This is a most unusual situation, and the article reads as follows:
Jamaican leaders are coming north next week for trade talks.
They want to step up buying in Canada to keep the vital sugar preference.
As it is now, $56 million goes from Jamaica to the U.S. annually, trade which could be diverted to Canada.
This is available to Canada. And the Jamaican slogan will be: If you've Got It, we'll Buy It.
The article goes on to make it very, very clear that they have all the dollars required in the Federation of the West Indies and that they feel because of their relationship with Canada in respect of the commonwealth and because of the assistance that Canada has been able to give them in respect of economic development and in trade preference that they have an obligation to Canada.
So we have these people almost pleading that we should export more in order that they may import less from the United States and so that we can see the kind of friends they are to us. Yet we have one hon. member who says, "Go slow-go slow, it is going to take a long while." On the other hand, the businessmen and the parliamentarians of Jamaica, according to the newspapers, are in a state of anxiety about trade with this country and we have such information as is

given to us in commercial letters and publications from financial organizations which I imagine are most stable, such as the Canadian Bank of Commerce.
When we view the entire picture, therefore, we must agree that this is the most appropriate time for the hon. member for Ottawa West to have introduced this motion for the expansion of trade with the Federation of the West Indies, and so far as this group is concerned we are most certainly heartily in agreement with its basic principles. Whether or not it is accepted by this House of Commons, we do suggest that something should be done to expand trade with the federation for which expansion the federation has been pleading and has outlined on more than one occasion.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bold and courageous decision of the ten British colonies of the Caribbean, Jamaica, Trinidad, Tobago, Barbados, the Leeward and Windward islands to form together a political federation was certainly an act of faith in themselves, in their land and in the commonwealth. It was a demonstration of faith in their ability to work together to develop their resources, to improve their living standards and to raise their level of prosperity; it was a demonstration of faith in the commonwealth because they knew their experiment could not hope to succeed without outside aid and that faith in the commonwealth was a demonstration of faith in Canada particularly because of all commonwealth countries Canada is the member in the best position to be able to give them the kind of assistance they need.
Following as they do a path similar to that followed by the Canadian provinces 90 years ago, they have every right to look to Canada for a large measure of assistance, not only because they subscribe to the same kind of parliamentary institutions and values as those to which we subscribe and because we are geographical neighbours, being part of the same hemisphere, not only because of Canada's tradition of assistance granted under the Colombo Plan, but most of all because, as the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) pointed out this afternoon, more than any other country in the world the economy of Canada supplements that of the British West Indies.
As the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Mac-quarrie) pointed out this afternoon, this federation faces tremendous difficulties, difficulties far more formidable than those faced by the Canadian provinces 90 years ago. These islands which have decided to federate extend over a range of some 1,800 miles and are separated by water; they have

the disadvantages of a small population with, in some areas, overcrowding. They have some cases of extreme poverty which did not obtain in Canada and to cope with all this they have less natural wealth to develop and upon which to draw.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has announced that a refrigerated ship will be built by Canada and given to the Federation of the West Indies as a gift for use in their inter-island trade, but more than that is required. They certainly require large amounts of capital investment and donations of capital goods; they need port and harbour facilities for loading and unloading cargoes; they need refrigeration facilities and technical know-how.
Above all, they will need ships to carry on trade between the British West Indies and Canada. These ships should be specially built for that purpose. We in Canada know the handicaps of having a small domestic market, and we can appreciate, therefore, that with a population of only around three million the British West Indies federation, if it is to develop and prosper, must rely mainly on the development of its external trade. Without the improvement and expansion of trade all our gifts of capital and equipment and other assistance will be of no use.
Canada has enjoyed trade relations with the British West Indies for over 200 years, and trade with the province of Newfoundland has probably extended over a longer period than that. This trade had its beginning with the maritime provinces and there are still great opportunities for its expansion to the mutual advantage of all Canada and particularly of the Atlantic region. We in Newfoundland have bought our supplies of rum-as the hon. member for Queens pointed out-from the West Indies, but we depend on them for other products too-staple products for our fishermen such as molasses and salt. Our manufacturing industries depend to a large extent on their bauxite, and the islands in turn depend upon Canada for dairy products, vegetables and manufactured goods.
Since 1912 there have been preferential trade agreements between Canada and the British West Indies federation. The original agreement of 1912 was revised in 1920 and again in 1926. In considering this resolution, which states that the government should consider the advisability of establishing free trade between Canada and the Federation of the West Indies, it would be worth while to take a look at the agreement which is already in existence. The present agreement grants prescribed margins of tariff preferences to most Canadian goods. The agreement provides that duties on Canadian
Canada-West Indies Trade goods may not exceed a certain percentage of most-favoured-nation rates of duties. For example, in the Barbados and Trinidad it must not exceed 50 per cent of the mostfavoured-nation rate; in Jamaica it must not exceed 75 per cent of that rate. To work out a practical example, if we suppose that in Trinidad the most-favoured-nation rate is 10 per cent, then the preferential tariff would not exceed 5 per cent. Similarly, in Jamaica it would not exceed 7| per cent. In addition, the agreement sets forth a specified margin of preference on Canadian flour, dairy products, meat, fish and apples.
Canada, under the agreement, grants free entry to most British West Indies products other than sugar, tobacco and spirits and bound margins of preference on all dutiable goods, including sugar. The most important preference is, of course, as the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) pointed out this afternoon, on raw sugar which is imported for refining in Canada and which forms the basis of manufacturing industries in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The preference on 96 per cent sugar is $1 per 100 pounds. Canada gave preferences also on bananas, cocoa beans, rum, coffee and spices and, in addition, gave a general undertaking that in respect of all goods not specifically mentioned in the agreement the duty on imports from the British West Indies would at no time exceed 50 per cent of the general tariff of Canada.
Notwithstanding the discriminatory dollar control restrictions, this agreement has greatly encouraged the growth of trade. If we look at the figures we find that for the three years immediately before the agreement was signed imports averaged $19 million a year; if we take the average for 1954, 1955 and 1956 we find that the average imports amounted to $58 million annually.
Now that the islands of the West Indies federation are working out their customs union it will be necessary for this trade agreement to be revised, and this appears to be a very opportune time for the government to give consideration to replacing this agreement by a free trade agreement. The present rates are so small as to have no significance as far as revenue is concerned, and the growth in trade which has already taken place indicates that an even greater expansion would result from a removal of restrictions altogether.
If we look at the year 1955 we find that Jamaica exported more to Canada than to the United States, and double what it exported to Europe. In the same year Trinidad exported to Canada twice as much as to the United States. On the other hand, the

Canada-West Indies Trade British West Indies have become Canada's third market for fully manufactured goods. Trade between Canada and the British West Indies must be a natural development, because the two economies supplement each other to a great degree; they produce things that we cannot produce and we produce products which they cannot produce. We need their products and they need ours, and trade under these conditions must necessarily be to our mutual advantage and certainly should be conducted as freely as possible.
As one who comes from Newfoundland I am particularly interested, naturally, in the expansion of the British West Indies market for our fish. This market has been one of our traditional salt fish markets for centuries. It is a necessary product because it provides these people with the essential protein and salt which are necessary to health in the kind of climate in which they live.
I wish to place some figures on the record to give some idea of the importance of this market for salt fish. We find that the exports to the Caribbean area for the years 1953 to 1957 inclusive represented 48 per cent of our total salt fish exports. Of that amount nearly half, or 21 per cent, went to the three larger islands which make up the British West Indies federation. Jamaica took an annual average of 113,000 quintals, Barbados an average of 23,000 quintals and Trinidad an average of 24,000 quintals making an average annual total of nearly 160,000 quintals of dried fish for each of the years between 1953 and 1957 inclusive.
With a growing population this market is bound to expand. It has been estimated that by 1970 the population of the British West Indies will have increased from 3,500,000 to 7 million. The best way to expand the market in that area not only for fish but for all Canadian products is to increase the prosperity of the people who consume. The implementation of this resolution will do a great deal more to make the British West Indies strong and prosperous and at the same time will benefit all Canada and particularly the Atlantic provinces. As far as the exportation of Newfoundland salt fish is concerned it would be more beneficial than a subsidy. The growth and prosperity of the British West Indies will strengthen not only the commonwealth but the whole free world. For that reason I have great pleasure in seconding the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Ottawa West. I commend him for bringing it forward at this time and I trust it will receive the support of all hon. members.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in rising to participate in this debate. Since I represent an agricultural constituency in the province of Saskatchewan I am naturally interested in any increase in trade since the area from which I come is also a surplus producing area. Although the West Indies federation has not yet come into being I feel that everything should be done within the present bounds of our trade agreements in order to increase the channels of two-way trade between Canada and this area.
According to the dominion bureau of statistics report of Canadian exports for March 1958, we are now exporting to the islands comprising the federation agricultural products of a wide variety. The exports represent practically ail phases of agriculture in Canada. It has been said today that the agricultural industries of both areas are complementary.
Representing a western constituency I am particularly interested in the volume of cereal grains and other field crops exported to the West Indies whether in the form of whole grain, flour or processed products such as macaroni, oil cake, poultry and stock concentrates. For years past the area comprising the West Indies federation has been a large and traditional market for Canadian wheat flour. Canadian flour has been sold and recognized as one of the economic links between the two members of the commonwealth. For the past few years the trend has been away from Canadian flour to United States flour due entirely to the subsidy being paid to United States mills enabling them to quote at prices Canadian mills cannot meet.
To illustrate this, in 1955 Canada exported 2,147,047 bags of flour, while in 1957 Canada exported 1,789,452 bags. To emphasize the fact that this change is due solely to United States subsidized flour, I quote from the report of the Canada flour export committee dated March 26 and prepared after a visit to Jamaica:
There Is a great deal of good will towards Canadian flour, and a desire to purchase counter grades if Canada could compete on price. Canadian baker's flour predominates, although there is evidence of American flour making inroads. American baking flour is selling at $4.62 to $4.82, with Canadian flour 40 cents to 50 cents a bag higher. The larger bakers point out the importance of high protein flour. Smaller bakers are mixing Canadian and American flour. The price differential on the American flour lowers their over-all cost and, unless steps are taken to remedy this condition, it is our feeling more and more American baker's flour will be used.
From the same source, with respect to Trinidad, I quote the following paragraph:
Flour from the United States of America mills has gained a strong position-so much so that one particular brand has become a criterion for all other brands. It was suggested by some importers that a new brand name common to all Canadian

mills and at a discount of 20 cents below the popular United States flour brand might be the answer. Flour is being offered by Canadian brokers as low as $4.25. This flour, however, is of a very indifferent quality, and is not giving Canadian flour a very good name. Canadian good quality flour would have to be sold at from 50 cents to 60 cents a bag below present offerings to create any interest. The bakers want a better grade of flour from Canada at a price of $4.40 c.i.f.
The two main classes of flour imported into the West Indies are baking flour and counter flour. Counter flour is imported almost 100 per cent from the United States because they are able to supply from that country a second clear flour of maximum 1 per cent ash'-protein does not matter-at a price which would be equivalent to about $3.40 Canadian per 100 pounds, c.i.f. Kingston, Jamaica. Although flour milled straight from Canadian No. 5 wheat was shipped to the West Indies a few years ago in large quantities and was found suitable for counter flour purposes, the present subsidy of the United States makes it impossible for any flour to be shipped from Canada at this price. Canada has maintained her position as a major exporter of flour through the years, not by selling cheap flour, but by selling quality. In commercial relationships with the West Indies, I feel sure that the Canadian milling companies stand well ahead of United States milling companies, yet we are losing business year after year. This is solely a matter of price. In 1957, Canada imported $58.4 million worth of goods from the British West Indies federation and exported to the islands $40.3 million worth of goods.
The solution of our flour export difficulties lies with our private enterprise people, with help from our trade commissioners. Already steps are being taken by the millers and the primary producers to introduce into the West Indies flour of a standard and at a price that will compete with United States subsidized flour. Wheat and flour exports to the West Indies are only part of the picture. To increase our exports we shall have to, and we can, take more of the West Indian agricultural products. The problem lies partly with the new federation and partly with ourselves. An exchange of ideas and of technical knowledge between the two countries is necessary. As the West Indian farmer learns to supply standard products to the market we shall see the West Indies seeking wider markets.
Another phase of their development is taken from the agricultural survey made by Dr. A. L. Jolly for the Caribbean commission. In discussing methods needed to improve agriculture, besides the one I mentioned, such as standardization of production to make available to exporters a standard product which would be acceptable, he has another 57071-3-157
Canada-West Indies Trade interesting comment to make. He mentions a difficulty which I think Canada can help to solve. In discussing the relationship of Caribbean agriculture and its industrial growth he states that Caribbean agriculture is inefficient, and to say that it is as efficient as any other tropical area is not good enough. He said:
-Caribbean agriculture is strikingly inefficient. Its inefficiencies are due primarily to lack of management. It is the function of management to organize the other economic factors of production in the most efficient combination. The characteristic of too much labour working with inefficient capital equipment, so typical of much Caribbean agriculture is due to the fact that management has not yet invented ways of righting this unbalance profitably. The lack of management is not due to lack of intelligence or lack of energy among managers but to their inadequate numbers. The problem in the Caribbean is not how a surplus of young trained men can find land and money to start farming, but who will replace the small number of existing managers when they retire.
There we have the problem facing the Caribbean agriculture which governments, private exporting companies and our universities can assist to solve by encouraging the training of young men and supplying and training the managers needed in this new area.
The West Indies federation, with a population of three million and with a very high birth rate, will never be able to produce sufficient food to feed its growing population. It is a population which will have a continuously rising standard of living. In this area we have at our door a market which should be ours. The great bulk of agricultural products from the British West Indies which will be seeking markets do not in any way conflict with our Canadian agriculture. On the other hand, as the British West Indies federation raises the standard and quantity of its products the United States will be forced by pressure groups within their economy to control the amount of those competing agricultural products entering the United States. This leaves Canada in a favoured position and gives us an opportunity to start to develop now a reciprocal trade in agricultural products, and we should take advantage of a situation which is so favourable to us.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. McGrath (St. John's East):
