speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks on this resolution will be brief because, since the outset of the debate, I have had the unhappy experience of sitting here and finding all the statistics which I have so long and laboriously sought after presented by previous speakers.
In his remarks, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) presented the problems of trade with the West Indies, particularly
2490	HOUSE OF
Canada-West Indies Trade as they apply to the province of Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces of Canada. It is interesting to note, that the salt fish industry, which is at present undergoing somewhat of a crisis, is accounted for by the most part by the provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, and one of the chief remaining customers of Canada's salt fish has been the British West Indies. We hope that the difficulties being encountered at present by the fish trades of the Atlantic provinces and the authorities of Jamaica and the other islands of the West Indies will soon be overcome so that we can settle back to our traditional happy trade relations with one of our best salt fish customers.
As was outlined by previous speakers, Canada and particularly the Atlantic provinces of Canada noted with interest the inaugural ceremonies last March founding what we hope will be one of the members of the commonwealth, the West Indies federation.
We in eastern Canada particularly were very much concerned with this development because, as I said previously, the West Indies are in fact one of our best customers. Perhaps it is ironic that we in the province of Newfoundland have had so many things in common with our neighbours in the new federation. For many years we have known the consequences, hardships and difficulties which flow from a single industry economy. We are also not unlike our neighbours in the West Indies in that much of our trade results from our geographical location.
I could not help but be impressed with the statistics that I encountered in my research, and particularly those statistics relating to salt fish. For example, of all the fish exported from Canada in 1957, 3.4 per cent went to the island of Jamaica which, incidently, comprises more than half the population of the new federation. The other nine islands are, by population and by size, small in comparison. My figures, therefore, for the most part deal with the island of Jamaica. Of the total fish exported in 1957-I believe this figure has already been cited on several occasions-6 per cent went to the British West Indies. I would venture to say that this 6 per cent came primarily from Newfoundland and Nova Scotia.
The resolution before us is an interesting one in that it advocates that the government consider the advisability of establishing a free trade area between Canada and the West Indies. This is most important to the Atlantic provinces of Canada, those provinces which have been struggling for so many years under many heavy problems. I noted with interest the remarks of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) and his suggestion that perhaps consideration might be given to


a Caribbean Colombo plan. This would seem to make sense in many ways, in so far as my limited experience goes. I hope it is a suggestion that will merit some consideration in the future. It is perhaps because the salt fish industry is of such importance that we on this side of the house have viewed with concern the problems of this industry which represents such an important part of the economy of the Atlantic provinces, particularly Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
I would suggest that this resolution merits the serious consideration of the members of the house. I would hope that in the debate which will follow the speakers will not be influenced by partisan politics, so that we may receive the utmost benefit from this very worthy suggestion.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first word in this debate must be to assess, in general, the picture that each country has of the other, that is the new Federation of the British West Indies as seen by Canadians and the reverse. I think that we each tend, in certain times of the year, to view the other as a paradise, especially when winter has cast its spell over our country and we tend to think of the sunny climate of the south and I think that they, with their fine weather, tend to think of Canada as the place to which they would like to come.
As the hon. member who preceded me has remarked, one of the disadvantages in participating in this debate is that everyone seems to have read that excellent publication called "Canada and the West Indies Federation", which was put out by Mount Allison University publications, at Sackville, New Brunswick, following an institute on Canada and the West Indies federation held last August. Actually, the full title is "Mount Allison 1957 Summer Institute, Canada and the West Indies Federation". To my horror I found that the mover of the resolution, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) began with a quotation from Sir Grantley Adams, then prime minister of the Barbados and now prime minister of the federation. When he stated, I am quoting from page 36, I started to say to myself, "But we are profoundly convinced-", and the hon. member for Ottawa West said, "But we are profoundly convinced-" and so on. He did neglect to give all the quotation, and I think it might be of interest to the house, so I have no hesitation in reading about 75 or 100 words from it.
But we are profoundly convinced that our whole future depends on the closest possible relationship with the Dominion of Canada. We have already passed appropriate resolutions at some of our federal meetings, and we intend in a short time to send delegations up to Ottawa. We are already determined to explore the possibilities for increased

trade and for increased immigration. Of course, we shall continue the cultural ties which have existed so long with Canada. When I was comparatively young, I think there were more McGill graduates among our doctors than from any other part of the world. Our youth comes to Canadian colleges and Canadian universities, and we want those ties to be strengthened and increased. I'm not flattering you, I'm not saying it because I'm addressing a Canadian audience, but I do say it; we consider our future success will lie with the closest possible understanding between the West Indies and Canada. We will do our best to make our contribution for mutual benefit as great as possible, and we confidently expect that this great dominion will do the same for the West Indies.
Those remarks, as I have indicated, were made by Sir Grantley Adams in his position as prime minister of the Barbados last August during the Mount Allison University summer institute. I was interested in the very thoughtful remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West, and the remarks of the other speakers who have followed him in this debate, concerning the general appreciation of the goods that are involved in trade between the federation and this country. I wonder if these speakers appreciate some of the grave problems that exist before trade can be opened up and expanded between Canada and the British West Indies federation. With that consideration in mind I should like to detail some of these problems as I go along in these brief remarks of this afternoon. Mainly they concern the problem of sterling.
The West Indies federation is a member of the sterling area. When I have concluded I should like to cast my remarks in such a way as to suggest to Canada that five years from now this whole matter of the federation down there will be surveyed by the component countries. They will decide whether they have been able to make this multilateral marriage work; whether the contract should be altered in any way; or perhaps even whether they should give up the idea altogether. Hence the developments over the next five years, Mr. Speaker, I think will be extremely important. It may yet be found that within that period of time we shall see the growth in Canada of a thought that here, far to the south of us, south of Halifax and Newfoundland, lies a country that could very nicely become the eleventh province of Canada.
I should now like to say a word about the traditional ties between our two countries. In 1892 the Department of Trade and Commerce came into being in the federal service. In that year 1892 Canadian commercial agents were appointed in Jamaica, Trinidad, Montserrat, St. Kitts, British Guiana and Barbados. In 1907 a Canadian trade commissioner was appointed at Bridgetown, Barbados and today there are two Canadian government trade commissioners in the West Indies, as was
57071-3-157J
Canada-West Indies Trade mentioned by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). I might point out that the office in Kingston covers the northern part of the federation, Jamaica, Bahamas and British Honduras, and included in the territory of the Port of Spain office is Barbados, Tobago, Trinidad, Windward and Leeward islands, British Guiana, French Guiana, Surinam, Guadeloupe and Martinique. Some of these, of course, are not particularly in the federation but that is the area served.
Last year the total Canadian trade with the West Indies amounted to about $99 million and last year the West Indies constituted the fourth largest market in the commonwealth for Canada. If we add these other places that I have mentioned, namely British Guiana, British Honduras, Bahamas and Bermuda, you will find that in 1957 this was the second largest market in the commonwealth for Canada, and our tenth market in the world.
These very elementary figures tend, I believe, to illustrate qualitatively the importance of this area in Canadian trade. Last year we sold $40 million worth of goods to the West Indies. In the past years about 85 per cent of Canada's exports to the West Indies has been in the class of manufactured or semi-manufactured goods. This, Mr. Speaker, is one of the highest ratios for any of our export markets, a point about which I intend to speak subsequently in my address this afternoon. We can compare this with our trade with the United Kingdom where only some 15 per cent to 20 per cent of our exports there are classed as manufactured or semi-manufactured.
In recent years there have been trade missions back and forth between Ottawa and the West Indies and probably there will be more. As you will recall, Sir Grantley, in his remarks at Mount Allison institute, said that trade delegations would be sent to this country. In recent years there has been the signing of the Canada-British West Indies trade agreement. We have seen the flow of British West Indies students to Canadian universities and nursing schools and of Canadian tourists to the West Indies, though I believe the tourist trade to the West Indies is primarily United States. Eighty-five per cent of the tourists there come from that country. Our realization of the importance of this federation is seen in the announcement of the gift of a new ship, which gift is contrasted with the strike on the Canadian National Steamships ships, and which gift cannot be construed as political because the Liberals thought of it and we are doing it.
But despite the trade which I have mentioned, the Canadian trade with this nation is not as large as it should be owing to

Canada-West Indies Trade several limiting factors. I think the consideration of these factors is important, for even if this house passes the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Ottawa West-and I hope we do-we must still remember that much remains to be done before that fine dream of free trade becomes the reality of free trade. I am also afraid that much of that cure will have to be found elsewhere than in Canada, and that it must be found within the unique trade structure of the federation itself.
As for the limiting factors in the amount of trade we can do, I think these points should be considered. The population is about 2.8 million. Their national income is low. Their productivity is low. The range of goods and services they offer for export is limited to the items that have been mentioned this afternoon including sugar, and its by-products, lumber, bauxite, oil and of course the various tourist facilities. Another factor is the competition which results for our trade in the West Indies. By tradition the United Kingdom has been the principal supplier. In recent years the West Indies, like other countries in the sterling area, have maintained restrictions on the import of dollar goods. As far as dollar exports are concerned, we must remember that the United States are closer and that they have the advantage owing to speed and the frequency of shipping, although the United States is at a disadvantage as compared with Canada because they do not receive the British preferential treatment.
Canadians also face competition from within the commonwealth and some of these countries are in the sterling bloc. New Zealand has built up a large market for cheese and butter which cuts into the prospects of this country and those of other suppliers. Australian flour has appeared on the market, and it seems rather odd when you think of bauxite going all the way from Jamaica to British Columbia and yet the reverse trip does not seem to pick up any of this western wheat about which there is so much debate in this house. Rather, they go to Australia for their flour; again, I imagine, because of the sterling factor. Many manufactured goods from European countries, from India, Japan and Hong Kong, are being sold in the West Indies federation and the Netherlands has increased its sales of canned beets and milk products.
Canadian goods are allowed into the West Indies under several categories. Those products under the world open general licence include onions, potatoes, split peas, fish except fresh and frozen fish, meat, cheese, kraft paper, newsprint, powdered and canned milk, animal feeding stuffs and lumber and in 1956 leaf tobacco, fresh apples, fertilizers and calcium carbide were added to the list of

goods which might be imported into the West Indies under the world open general licence. The West Indies trade liberalization plan embraces a second group designed to maintain traditional markets of exports to this area and the way it works is that Canadian exporters of products listed under the plan are entitled to apply for allocations on the basis of their exports to that area between the years 1946 and 1948.
The annual report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for 1957 contains at page 52 several paragraphs on the operations of the British West Indies trade liberalization plan and perhaps I can take some brief excerpts from this report. The number of firms participating in the plan last year was 722; individual allocations processed and issued by this section during the year were 8,005, or an increase of about 35 per cent over 1956. That, of course, is an indication of the intense interest in Canada in this market to our south.
Some new products, of course, have been manufactured since this period 1946 to 1948, and the department has over the years made some provision to grant special allocations to firms which were not in business during that period and to grant them special allocations under special circumstances. Imports of products other than those in the two classifications I have mentioned, the first being the world open general licence and the second the West Indies trade liberalization plan, are subject to individual licensing. The component colonies each have a dollar program under which they grant licences for dollar goods considered essential to the development of the country and some of these colonies operate special dollar import schemes whereby dollar import quotas are distributed among local importers, thus enabling them to import Canadian or United States goods of their own choosing.
Mention has been made of the Canadian goods supplied to the West Indies, which perhaps might be broken down regionally as follows; from the west coast, lumber, apples and canned salmon; from the prairie provinces, flour; from Ontario and Quebec, motor vehicles, milk products, flour and feeds, paint, pharmaceuticals, footwear, paper, textiles, beer, rubber goods and general manufactured goods; and from the maritime provinces- and in these I include our latest acquisition, Newfoundland-salt, pickled and canned fish, potatoes, grocery items, shoes and other consumer goods.
Mention was also made this afternoon by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and I believe by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) of some of

the problems of fish exporting trade to the West Indies. This matter is again covered in the excellent little book to which I referred earlier, entitled "Canada and the West Indies Federation". At page 72 of this publication the author of the article "The Fish Trade", Mr. R. F. Johnson, secretary of the Canadian Atlantic fish exporters association, remarks:
There is good reason to believe that past preferential tariff treatment of B.W.I. products by Canada, has led to curtailment in sales of our salt and pickled fish to some non-commonwealth Caribbean countries without resulting in compensatory increases in our sales of fish to the B.W.I.
He goes on to explain what is going on as follows:
The largest salt fish market in the B.W.I., Jamaica, maintains a consumer price ceiling on salt cod notwithstanding that within recent weeks a government minister of Jamaica is reported to have said publicly that "the Canadian sugar market is vital to our existence". This ceiling price, which applies to all five sizes of both choice and standard grades of salt cod, indirectly determines the prices that our Canadian fishermen receive for their salt cod production-and which price we have already shown is inadequate. In December 1953, this ceiling price in Jamaica was reduced from Is. 7Jd. to Is. 6d, and it was further reduced in June 1955, to Is. 5d. Only following repeated representations, including a delegation from the Canadian industry travelling to Jamaica to discuss the matter with government officials, was the ceiling price increased in September, 1956, to the current Is. 6id. per pound, still Id. below the pre-December, 1953, level.
And so on and so on.

I was trying to illustrate my point that we are going to run into some difficulty when Canadians and members of the British West Indies federation get
Canada-West Indies Trade together to discuss ways and means of increasing trade between the two countries. I did not intend to get into a discussion which would be esoteric to me regarding the problems of the fishing industry and I hope this answer will reassure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that I am not trying to horn in on the speciality of those who come from fish producing communities.
I mentioned earlier the fact that we supplied the West Indies with an astonishingly high percentage of manufactured goods in our exports to them-some 80 or 85 per cent-which is most unusual in ordinary trade dealings. This brings me to a most vital point, and I will illustrate it by the aluminum development in Canada and the bauxite development in the British West Indies. It should be noted that it has been Canadian investment in bauxite mining which has made possible a large export of this mineral to Canada. Trinidad's exports of petroleum products can be traced back to the first commercial discovery of oil in that colony by a Canadian syndicate at the turn of the century. Today Canadian interests are looking at copper and other mineral possibilities in Jamaica, and Canadian capital is moving into the hotel industry on Jamaica's north coast with a view to attracting more Canadian tourists.
The magazine called Commonwealth Development at page 27 of its March-April issue, volume 5, No. 2 makes an interesting point in an article called "Economic Outlook for the Federation", and I quote:
It will be the policy of the federation to assist the islands to increase the variety of their crops and also to hasten the development of secondary industries. It is in the secondary industries, assisted by a tax relief scheme, that there is the greatest scope for joint capital ventures and co-production with British firms, as is happening, for example in soap and in paint manufacture. Other secondary industries include the manufacture of margarine, matches, shoes, garments, leather and fancy goods and fruit canning.
The magazine Commonwealth Development is a British publication, and hon. members will note, in the quotation I have just read, that great emphasis was laid on the possibility for British investment in the Federation of the West Indies. I think we can substitute the word "Canadian" in that context for "British". Perhaps as partners with them there is ample room to develop this sprawling area which has now become a federation, and I think this is something that should definitely be kept in mind, knowing that in the past our investments in petroleum and bauxite have led to the development of mutually profitable industries.
I said earlier that at the end of five years the Federation of the West Indies will take stock of how this multi-lateral marriage of

Canada-West Indies Trade the various islands has worked out. What the assessment will be, time alone can tell.
I think Canada should keep a close eye on the developments there, and give these people the most sympathetic consideration and all the help we possibly can; and I think, too, that some day we should even consider asking them to become one of our own provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to comment on the remarks which have been made earlier in this debate, before I come to my own contribution which will be made on behalf of the industrial areas of Canada, particularly the most noted, outstanding and progressive area of Canada, the Toronto area -whether the future of trade with the British West Indies federation follows the pattern suggested by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) or not.
It has occurred to me several times during this debate that the ideas and contributions which have been made to it are certainly varied in their sources. As I was waiting my turn to speak, that great paper the Ottawa Journal came to my desk and I noticed an article there headed: "Labour party urges Colombo plan type commonwealth aid". The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) will be surprised to find himself in the company of such political bedfellows. I should like to read briefly from this short article:
The British Labor Party Saturday night proposed the establishment of organizations similar to those of the Colombo Plan to aid underdeveloped areas of the commonwealth.
It said the Colombo Plan, devised to boost food production and provide educational facilities in underprivileged Asian countries, could be used as a model for similar work in Africa and the West Indies.
The party's policy pamphlet said Canada and the United States-both members of the Colombo Plan -would be invited to take part in the new project if a Labor government is returned in the next British elections.
I hope, incidentally, that developments along these lines will not have to wait for anything such as that, an event, which, I am confident, is far in the distant future.
To get back to comments concerning other contributions to this debate, I must say that when I was advised that this resolution was to come up today, and took my seat here, I began to wonder if, in fact, the resolution had come up after listening to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Ottawa West. He spoke of pessimism abroad as far as Canada's future trade developments are concerned, and I find it hard to justify that remark or agree with it in any measure. Perhaps it was just the labouring of other political remarks he made. The hon. member

also suggested that the great Liberal party had been responsible for everything-I suppose as part of the process commonly emanating from those benches-an attempt to rewrite the history of Canada and leave notable periods out.
Fortunately, the present political situation in Canada has corrected a good deal of that way of thinking. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) spoke of the need for capital goods, in particular, and I expected him to go on and mention the concessions that have been made and the encouragement provided in the West Indies with respect to the types of industry guaranteed to promote employment in that area, and certainly here is a field in which Toronto manufacturers and particularly producers of capital goods are finding interesting new prospects. Another thing which struck me about the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East is that he used what has hitherto been a nasty word in that quarter of the house, the word "diversion".
He spoke of it in a most favourable way. I notice that the hon. member is looking rather puzzled. He will recall his quotation from the Financial Post in which it was proposed to divert purchases from the United States to Canada.

speechtext:
But you seemed pleased about it. The remarks of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) were, I thought, most appropriate and fitting as most of his contributions to the debates of this house during my experience have been. The suggestion advanced by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) concerning the eleventh province I find very attractive. A very good friend and sometimes a political companion of mine at the university referred to presented to the federation on behalf of Canada a chair which had once been the property of Sir John A. Macdonald, which greatly added to the spirit of that occasion. I refer, of course, to the gesture by Professor Ian L. Campbell.
One aspect of the relationship of Canada to the West Indies which was not touched upon and which I expected would be raised 

and I anticipate it will be dealt with by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, he having had it within his purview over the years-is the question of immigration and immigration quotas from that area. Overpopulation has been mentioned by one or two speakers thus far in this debate. I would suggest to the government that it review the question of immigration quotas from that area. I think this would do far more than

many other friendly gestures made to the federation to promote a feeling of good will, and the promise of future good relations between Canada and the West Indies.
Referring again to Toronto, the hon. member for Ottawa West implied that nothing was being done concerning trade with the West Indies and that the situation was static. I should like to point out that certainly in my experience that is not the case. The volume of correspondence I have had from businessmen in Toronto inquiring about trade possibilities in the West Indies certainly gives the lie to that statement. I suppose that my friends in the corner, the lonesome eight, will be a little chagrined to know that the spirit of free business enterprise is stepping into the gap and providing its own incentive in this matter without the benefit of government boards and similar bodies. There have been a number of businessmen in the Toronto area making investigations of the possibilities as far as exports to the West Indies are concerned.
The quotation I should like to place on the record in concluding my remarks is taken from the publication entitled "Foreign Trade", October 26, 1957 issue. It deals with business conditions in the Caribbean. I should like in particular to refer to a paragraph entitled, "Investment Opportunities Worth Study" which reads as follows:
The most pressing need for these islands is capital for development and know-how and there are a number of opportunities for investment that might appeal to Canadian businessmen. Among them are building and running hotels or other types of accommodation for tourists in all of the islands; small industries processing local produce into jams, preserves, chutney and sauces, canned fruits and fruit juices; leather tanning; cocoa and chocolate manufacture; poultry farming to supply eggs and dressed fowl, and fibre processing.
This is the key paragraph:
Canadians with money to invest should take a pleasure-cum-business trip down to appraise the situation at first hand.
This is the type of thing which I mentioned as having been greatly activated during the last year. I continue:
The various governments welcome such visits and provide all the pertinent information on income tax concessions to pioneer industries and on the co-operation they are prepared to give. Included in this is the duty-free entry of capital equipment necessary to get the projects started.
Canadians who wish to establish a business in an area with a year-round summer climate should turn their attention to the British West Indies. They will find great good will towards Canadians, the result of a long and mutually profitable association.
In looking to the future of the British West Indies, particularly in light of the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway which
Canada-West Indies Trade will so soon be upon us, I see every indication of tremendously increased development in exports from Canada consistent with the policies of this government in matters of trade.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few observations I should like to make about this motion. This is the second private members' day of the session and I felt it would perhaps be inappropriate for one who had once occupied the treasury benches to put himself forward while there were new members who wished to take part in the debate. I have therefore been waiting in the hope that perhaps by listening to the new members my own speech would be greatly shortened and I think it will be because there seems to be agreement, at least among all those who have spoken, about the desirability of supporting the motion which the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) introduced so effectively this afternoon.
I have no thought or intention of introducing a note of controversy in this matter. I hope that before this sitting day is over the house will register approval of this motion. I do not mean to suggest that we should have a division and indeed I would hope that would not be necessary. It is my hope that we will formally adopt the motion of the hon. member for Ottawa West.
The motion merely asks us to say:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of establishing free trade between Canada and the Federation of the West Indies.
If we were all to approve formally of this motion I do not believe it would impose any obligation upon the government to do anything forthwith except to give active consideration to this question which I hope and am inclined to believe the government is doing already. I have some hope in that respect from what was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) himself in presenting his estimates. One section of the presentation given by the minister which I found very sympathetic was what he said about West Indian trade, and I should like him to know that.
I think it might be a good idea for this house to pronounce itself in favour of this proposition at this particular time in this particular session since we know there is to be a conference in Montreal in September of the commonwealth countries at which the Federation of the West Indies is to be represented, I understand, by observers, but where there will be presumably the leading figures from the West Indian federation present who will be not only taking part in those
2496	HOUSE OF
Canada-West Indies Trade deliberations but will be having an opportunity to meet and talk once more with leading members of the government and our officials.
We know, of course, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) was one of the three members of the government who represented this country at the inauguration of the parliament of the federation only a very short time ago, and I am sure that most of those in the Federation of the West Indies who have the responsibilities, which are as the hon. member for Ottawa West and I think every subsequent speaker pointed out, still diffused through the federation and not concentrated in the federal government or federal parliament, for trade matters, will be present.
I of course agree with what the hon. member for Ottawa West said about the trade agreement of 1926, which is still the agreement which governs our trade relations with the West Indies federation. While I agree that it was a great step forward at that time, I think nearly all of us who have had any familiarity with the problems of trade with that area in recent years, particularly in the last year or two, have reached the conclusion that that agreement is out of date; that it no longer covers the kind of trading conditions that have to be met in this world in which we are faced with an increasing trade war between the communist world and the free world, and with an increased tendency toward the formation of trade blocs even in the free world.
Preferences alone are obviously not good enough. That does not mean to say for a moment I am suggesting that the historic preferences should be done away with; far from it. What I feel is, if we are to increase our trade with the West Indian federation, which is already a considerable part of the total trade of Canada-as has been pointed out several times they are our second best customer in the commonwealth and the tenth best customer in the world-if we are to increase that trade substantially and as rapidly as we would like and to meet the kind of competition which, as I pointed out the other day on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, has already done us out of the market for fish in Jamaica, we will obviously have to take other steps more in line with the modern conditions. I am sure the government is giving consideration to those steps.
There is one note of warning that I had rather expected and had rather thought the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), who spoke a little while ago, might have sounded himself when he was speaking. He


quoted an earlier statement by Mr. Johnson, the secretary of the Canadian Atlantic salt fish exporters association. I interrupted him and drew attention to the statement which was made by Mr. Zwicker, the president, and Mr. Johnson, the secretary, of that association which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald on July 12. I am not going to take the time of the house by reading it, but there is one point in it that does deserve careful consideration. We have a very big market for salt fish in the Caribbean area outside the British West Indies, in Cuba, in Puerto Rico and in the Dominican Republic and I believe now to some degree in Panama. We value that market. Over the years it has been a very good market and, by taking steps that might seem to be of an unfair or discriminatory nature, we do not want to take any risk of losing it. It is something that I know the government would keep very much in mind in any arrangements it might make for the increase of trade with the British West Indies; but we do want also to maintain and to expand our trade with those other Caribbean areas and particularly to maintain a fish market without which, of course, the fishing industry would be in a very depressed state indeed.
I think, too, that most of us-and the hon. member for Ottawa West made this pretty clear in what he said-would agree that it is not by tariff action mainly that we would achieve the kind of results we would hope to see achieved. That, I imagine, is why the hon. member for Ottawa West phrased his motion the way he did that the government should consider the advisability of establishing free trade rather than establishing a free trade area. If he had used the phrase a "free trade area", which has a certain technical connotation, it might have seemed rather more restrictive and exclusive than I think or hope he had in mind. What I think he had in mind was that he would like to see at any rate as an ultimate goal the removal of all tariffs between Canada and the British West Indies but that he would like also to see-and certainly speaking for myself I would like to see

us take other and more positive measures for the promotion of a greater flow of trade and a freer flow of trade between Canada and that area.
Now, I did make a suggestion on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce which I believe it would be trespassing on the time of the house now to repeat in any detail today. I would just remind hon. members that what I suggested was that the Canadian National West Indies Steamships, if the government had reached a firm conclusion-as they say they have-not to attempt

to have them operated under Canadian registry by Canadian National Railways any longer; if that decision cannot be changed- of course, we would like to see it changed; we would like to see them operate under the Canadian flag, as we intended to operate them if we had remained in office-but if the Canadian government's decision-I do not want to be controversial about this-seems to be that it is irrevocable, then I suggest they give very serious consideration to retaining the ownership of those ships but transferring them under some mutual aid arrangement to the Federation of the West Indies, to be operated on the same service, or at least over the same area, from the West Indies to Canada.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was recalling the suggestion I made to the government on Saturday that they give consideration to the possibility of maintaining title to these Canadian National (West Indies) ships, and transferring them under some kind of mutual aid or other similar arrangement to the West Indies federation, in order that these shipping services might be preserved between Canada and the West Indies. I know that there might be some difficulties about the operation for the first year or two under this arrangement, but looking to the steadily rising population both there, and we hope in Canada, and to the expansion of trade we could reasonably anticipate over the years it should not be very long, if they could be reasonably efficiently operated, before these ships would be carrying a considerably increased volume of goods between the two areas. Of course, there is no real use in talking about the expansion of trade between these two areas which are geographically a long way apart across the water, unless there is reliable and efficient and reasonably cheap transport.
I did mention the other day the speech that was made by the head of the Atlantic Acadia sugar refinery at Saint John, New Brunswick, in which he pointed out, I assume correctly, that the freight rate from Jamaica to Saint John was 46 cents and to the St. Lawrence 50 cents. This, in itself, was a very considerable factor that had to be weighed by this company in deciding whether it could continue its operations in Saint John. It does seem to me, that anything we can do to prevent the removal of this historic industry 57071-3-158
Canada-West Indies Trade from Saint John would be, if it could be justified at all in relation to the cost, well worth doing. We know that there are a number of industries in the maritime provinces which depend upon the refining of sugar in those provinces for their raw materials in their own fabrication. I am thinking of such a firm as Ganong's, for example.
It did occur to me that it might be possible, if these ships were operated from the West Indies to Saint John, from Saint John to Halifax, and from Halifax to St. John's, then directly back to the West Indies, this would be the shortest route they could take to cover all those areas. It would be the route in which, so far as one can see now, there would be the maximum amount of traffic. It may very well be that with this new piggy-back development in the railways, and with reasonable refrigeration in these ships, some new developments in the transportation of fruit and vegetable from the West Indies would make them more competitive. Commodities of that sort, which depend on a reasonable degree of speed in getting to the market, logically would be shipped to Saint John and transported by rail to central Canada from there, thus reversing some of the trends that have been all too prevalent in our transportation in the past.
I cannot forbear, mentioning again the feeling that is quite universal in Newfoundland, that some means should be found to equalize the freight on salt fish between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland on the one hand and the West Indies on the other. Unhappily today most of the Newfoundland fish has to be shipped to Halifax and transshipped there, thus adding very considerable to the cost of transporting Newfoundland fish and reducing the return to the producer of the fish. It had been the hope of many of us that the West Indies steamships, if they had continued to operate, would have operated out of St. John's, Newfoundland. Of course on the route between Halifax and Saint John and St. John's, Newfoundland, there is always lots of freight in the form of, manufactured goods of one kind and another, going to the Newfoundland market.
I want to turn next to what after all has been, in the years since the war, the principal obstacle to the expansion of our trade to the degree we would like to have seen it expand with the West Indies. I refer to the exchange controls and the dollar shortage in the sterling area. This problem has resulted in the restriction particularly of the exports of manufactured goods from Canada to the West Indies. I was rather surprised to hear what the hon. member for Vancouver East
2498	HOUSE OF
Canada-West Indies Trade (Mr. Winch) said this afternoon in his otherwise admirable speech. I cannot believe that he could have been correctly informed when he said the Jamaicans and other British West Indians were clamouring for things to buy in Canada. Although there has been some considerable easing in those restrictions, thanks to repeated representations made by the previous government and the present government, there is still, as I understand it, a good deal of difficulty about the free entry of our goods into this area because of exchange controls.
It has seemed to me that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) put his finger on this problem in a speech he made in the house on January 7, 1958, as reported at page 2970 of Hansard. These sentences were quoted by the hon. member for Ottawa West in introducing this motion, but I should like to quote them again because I want to speak particularly about one aspect of the matter. What the Leader of the Opposition said was:
Perhaps it would be worth considering whether we cannot tie that new part of the commonwealth-
He was referring to the West Indies.
-as it soon will become, more closely economically and financially, to our own country, Canada, by exploring the possibility of free trade between the West Indies and Canada, or a freer trade area, and by tying up our two currencies-[DOT]
It is this I want to emphasize at the moment.
-which would encourage trade and transport between us.
We all know, of course, that the fact that Newfoundland, for many years before confederation, was within the Canadian monetary system did have an enormous effect in maximizing the trade between Newfoundland and Canada. We also know that when, because of the completion of confederation in 1949, Newfoundland came within the Canadian customs area, that trade increased at least fourfold in a very few years. Since Newfoundland was, before confederation, one of Canada's largest and most valuable customers, we can see clearly how the removal of barriers of this sort does, in fact, promote trade.
I will admit it would be difficult to contemplate bringing the West Indies within the Canadian monetary system without our accepting some responsibility at the same time for the governmental deficits which are likely to exist in that area during the first few years of the federation. But I would remind hon. members that if we do not bear the burdens of these deficits, the British will have to bear them. As long as the British government and the British taxpayers are expected to bear that burden, it is not unreasonable for them to claim, in compensation for it, that


they should have the kind of control they now exercise over the external trade of that area.
While I should not like to express a categorical view about this matter, it seems to me that it would be worth the while of the government and particularly of the department of the Minister of Trade and Commerce-the minister who has charge of maximizing our external trade-to make a careful study of what would be likely to be accomplished by bringing this area within the Canadian monetary system and at the same time accepting some of the responsibility that the British government is now accepting for the potential deficit of the government of that area.
We all know, of course, that for years Canadian banks have been operating in the British West Indies, and doing so very well. The fact that this area represents a tenth of our customers is in no small part owing to the initiative taken by the Canadian banks in going into this area. We also know that undoubtedly the greatest need of the West Indies area, like that of every other undeveloped area in the world, is the need for additional capital.
I must say that I was particularly pleased to hear the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) this afternoon join with other members who have spoken and with other members from Newfoundland in supporting the proposal which I believe was first made by the premier of Newfoundland at the time the Gordon commission was sitting in that province namely that we should have in Canada a little Colombo plan or something of that sort for the West Indies. It seems to me that there is no other area in the world from which Canada could gain so much, directly and indirectly, as it could from this area with a plan of that sort.
The hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) this afternoon raised the very thorny question of the overpopulation of this area. It is true, of course, that the population in the West Indies has grown by leaps and bounds. There are over 3 million within the federation at the present time. The fact that there is not enough industrial development means that there is in this area a lack of opportunity for employment for that number of people. However, I think the only effective and helpful way of finding employment for those people in that area is from greater capital development. It seems to me that if Canada could take the lead in this field we could, directly and indirectly, secure a great return for any investment that was made, either publicly or privately, as long as it was wisely done.

This is one vision which I would commend to the government and particularly to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is a vision that has always attracted the Canadians in the Atlantic provinces. I should like to remind the house of these facts. The West Indian market is vital to the fish producers of Canada. Though the West Indian market is extremely important to other producers of raw materials such as lumber, wheat and potatoes; the biggest of our exports to the West Indies, when trade is relatively free, is in manufactures. Hence it would not be just for the Atlantic provinces or for Saskatchewan that this market, if it could be expanded, would be a good thing; it would also be good for the great manufacturing area of central Canada, as was rightly pointed out by the hon. member for York-Scarborough when he made his contribution to the debate.
It seems to me that there is, of course, another area in that same region that we must take into account in any proper long range plans for the development of the British West Indies. I refer, of course, to Demerara or British Guiana. This area is certainly not overpopulated. It has a great area with vast resources barely tapped. When I was minister of citizenship and immigration, in discussion with one of the ministers from Demerara, I learned that the authorities there do not feel that they are overpopulated. What they feel is that they are starved for capital. They look upon that great country-and it is a great country with a huge area many times that of all the British West Indies-as a potential field for a marriage between capital from North America and settlers from the West Indies. In any large long range plans for the development of this area and for the development of freer trade, I feel that our relations with Demerara and the relations of Demerara with the federation would require to be taken into account. In Demerara there is a vast hinterland and in the West Indies there are people who are nearest to it and who are already adapted to living in that part of the world.
I feel that in the whole field of external trade there is perhaps no more imaginative conception than that of bringing this whole area not merely within the trade orbit but within the financial and economic orbit of Canada. As has been pointed out over and over again in this debate on both sides of the house, in all quarters of the house, there is hardly a commodity produced in this area that is competitive with anything produced in Canada. They need our products and we need theirs. It is one of those rare things, an almost perfect combination. Moreover, there is a long tradition going back at least a 57071-3-158|
Canada-West Indies Trade couple of centuries and perhaps more; although perhaps when we go back beyond two centuries we would not want to revive some of the trade that existed at that time; but for two centuries there has been the kind of trade that we should like to see extended. There have been personal relationships between Canadians, particularly in the Atlantic provinces, and the people of the West Indies which play a large part in the development of trade.
There is, of course, the banking system of Canada already there. There is a long and excellent record of work done by the trade commissioner service of our own government. There are the constant visits back and forth. There are the thousands-and I am sure I do not exaggerate in using that word-of students who over the years have come from that area to attend our universities, some of whom, of course, get a taste for living in Canada when they come here and do not want to go back. None of us can blame them for that. But if we could do something to make the economic climate in that region such that these people would want to go back to develop a great new country for their own people, it seems to me that we would have there a conception of something that would be mutually fruitful both to us and to them.
These are some of the reasons. As I said when I began, I do not want to take an undue amount of time in repeating things that have been said just as well, if not better, by other members, some of them newcomers in the house. Once again may I say this. Perhaps it will not make much difference one way or another to the government of Canada whether or not we pass this resolution because the members of the government are, I believe, considering this problem anyway. It is inevitable that they are considering it and I think from the hints given to us by the Minister of Trade and Commerce they are seriously considering it, but it does seem to me that it would not have much effect one way or the other, so far as the government is concerned, if we pass this motion. But its effect on the country, particularly on the Atlantic provinces, in offering new hope to our people would infuse new vigour into the old search for mutual trade. It would also offer great hopes to the people of the Federation of the West Indies. This would be particularly so if the parliament of Canada unanimously adopted a resolution of this character. I am sure this would greatly strengthen the arm of the minister when he meets these people face to face in September, true, it will be in a rather unofficial capacity, but still he will meet them face to face. I have reference, of course, to the conference
2500	HOUSE OF
Canada-West Indies Trade in Montreal at which time he would be able to say to them, "I can talk to you frankly and freely because I know from the sentiments expressed on both sides of our parliament that we really want to do everything we can to develop closer economic ties and freer trade and we are willing to do everything necessary to realize this objective."
I think, having said this, that I should now take my seat in the hope that the debate will not be prolonged beyond the end of the present sitting and that we may unanimously register our approval of this proposition, which I am happy to say has so far found no dissenter in the house.

speechtext: I would not want to get into any kind of argument with the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) on this subject because, to be quite honest about it, I do not know the answer to his question. I suspect, of course, that the rates set on the Canadian National ships, would be within the control of the Canadian government but the rates about which Mr. Hill the head of this company, was talking were probably not on Canadian National ships. I do not know who set them or upon what basis they were set. As I made quite clear both on Saturday and today, I do not even know for sure whether Mr. Hill's facts were correct and I do not pretend to have verified them. I suspect they are correct and I suspect they are probably set to be, in some degree, competitive but it would not be the first time that things had been done in a positive way by the Canadian government in order to overcome some of our disadvantages in the realm of transportation in the Atlantic provinces. Even if the government were to intervene-at least for a time-to set a rate which would be competitive, I am not sure that I would not perhaps be inclined to vote for that subsidy with perhaps a little more enthusiasm than with respect to others which from time to time we are called upon to approve in this house in order to keep the balance of the Canadian economy.

May I ask
the hon. member how the federal government could intervene in respect to private shipping rates?

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext: But this is water shipping.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext: I do not know that there is any real difference in principle between having a subsidy on shipping on water rather than on land. Indeed I would have thought there were many and hoarier precedents for subsidies on water transportation than there were on land transportation.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in making this, my maiden contribution in this house, I hope you will permit me to extend to you my congratulations on the unanimous election to your position of first commoner. I do not want to have this remark on the record as a mere formality because, from my own observation since the opening of the session on May 12 last, I know that you fill your position with evidence of great character, with great tact, with ability to understand and to speak fluently in both languages used in this house and in a manner which brings confidence to a new and trembling member rising for the first time in this chamber. I know, sir, from my own observations that I shall receive from you guidance and, when necessary, discipline, which I will willingly accept. I would also at this time like to congratulate the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Sevigny) and the Deputy Chairman (Mr. Rea).
I do not intend to refer to all the things I have ferreted out in the library and from information obtained from the Department of Trade and Commerce, from the many periodicals at which I have looked and from the information already placed on the record. I do not think it is necessary to be on one's feet all the time permitted in order to accomplish one's objective and in so far as the facts which have been placed on the record with respect to this particular resolution are concerned, I am hoping that those facts will reduce the length of time during which I shall have to burden the house.
Coming from Regina, however, I was excited by this resolution because it had to do with trade, and I think it goes without saying that whether one is a Tory, a Liberal or a member of the C.C.F. trade is of paramount interest to all western members.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Our economy in the west
demands that we be a trading nation and for many years the symbol of that economy has been the grain elevator. The horizons of western Canada today, I am glad to say, are changing because we now have in company with these grain elevators oil derricks and to that extent our economy has been diversified and further stabilized.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the contributions with respect to this resolution. I wish to say quite frankly that when I first read the resolution and I realized that its sponsor came from a party which had been in power for 22 years I was very suspicious of it, suspicious as to the reason why it had been placed on the order paper at this time, and of the language in which it had been placed there. This was because for years I have not heard of Liberal members speaking in support of free trade but now that the Liberal party is out of office and sitting in the opposition benches its members are, one might say, taking their first opportunity to speak in support of free trade. This is when they have no responsibility as a government and when they can hit the press with big headlines and endeavour to maintain that old bogey that the Tory party is the party of high tariffs and the Liberal party is the party of free trade. That is something with which I completely disagree and I have been doing some research on this subject-

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext: You will need it.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
I do not need perhaps to do too much more research work, and I hope to have an opportunity in the not too distant future to put on record the facts in connection with tariffs in Canada, the facts as to which party is the party of high tariffs and which is the party of low tariffs. To me it seems to be just common sense that tariffs should neither constitute a merit to one party or a demerit to another. All parties who have held power in this parliament of Canada have at times imposed tariffs, and over the years the tariff structure has grown; it is not, of course, just because we have had a Liberal government for these last 22 years. But I will not take up the time of the house now by going into this question. If I did go into detail I think I could put on record a story very different from the one we hear from time to time.
The part of this resolution which excited me, as I said, was the part dealing with trade, and that is what I want to speak about because I come from a city which is a great trading centre of the prairies, the queen city of the prairies. I do not see the hon. member
Canada-West Indies Trade for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) in his place, but I think it is the fastest growing city, percentage-wise of population, and it depends for its economic well-being on agriculture and on trade. In my researches I found that wheat flour plays a considerable part in the trade between Canada and the West Indies. It was hard to get exact figures. Certainly I do not pretend that my figures are correct as applied to the West Indian federation as it exists today. I found, while I was doing research, that many others were doing research too and that material which I needed was in the hands of others, and probably material which others needed was in my hands. But in regard to wheat flour, I found that in 1953 Canada exported 2,183,872 bags to the islands of the West Indies, while in the same year the United States exported 413,833 bags. In 1955, 2,147,047 bags entered from Canada and 1,195,000 from the United States. In 1957, 1,504,250 were exported from Canada and 1,760,969 from the United States.
It is easy to talk about this being a traditional market. In many instances, over the years, the tastes and requirements of the West Indies have changed, and that in turn has brought about changes in the amounts and values of some of these goods which they import from Canada. But as against a diminishing desire for some products there has been an increasing desire for wheat flour. In 1955, the market, according to the figures of exports from Canada and the United States alone, increased by 744,342 bags. The Canadian share of this market dropped by 36,825 bags and the United States share increased by 781,167 bags. In 1957, according to the figures I found, there was a decrease in the market, compared with 1955, of 76,828 bags. Canadian sales decreased 642,798 bags. United States sales in that same year increased by 565,969 bags despite the decrease in the overall market. Inasmuch as the figures indicate there is still a desire among the people of the West Indies for wheat flour, I would point out that we still have wheat in great surplus; we want to dispose of it to any market that requires it, provided we can trade honourably. Even though small quantities are concerned, we cannot afford to lose this opportunity.
I thought the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) made a very fine contribution to this debate. It seemed to me, in the course of his remarks, that it was notable that he probably does not agree with the precise wording of the resolution, because he seldom-perhaps only once or twice-spoke about free trade. In the main he used the

Canada-West Indies Trade phrase "freer trade". It seems to me it is impossible, by any unilateral action, to have free trade. It is probably impossible for bilateral action to ensure it.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Did he fail to hear me when I said I should like to see tariffs between us wiped out.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext: Yes, but I gathered from all your contributory remarks that you figured it was quite impossible.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext: I am much more hopeful than that.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman served in a government which was in power for many years, and he has witnessed the decline in Canadian flour exports, and I thought he was being more realistic. And now he is trying to disturb my remarks and draw me off the track.
I say in all seriousness that this is one instance where the agricultural people of the prairies can come here with a sound case and ask for co-operation and consideration from all people in Canada. We need this market for this flour, and, as I understand it, with one exception we have always shipped the very best grade of flour to this market. In the first instance the market demand was a demand for baking flour which was used by the industry there. Then the people began to buy what is called counter flour, and used it for making bannocks or whatever they might call them. Now, the United States is, I understand, supplying to that market a grade which they do not even offer on their own market, and they do it on a subsidized basis.
I wish to commend this government for standing up and tackling the problem which the United States disposal policy has presented in the traditional markets of Canada, and I do not know any more pointed example than this putting forward of a special grade of flour on a subsidized basis, as is done in this market. The loss of sales to Canada is certainly something to be alarmed about. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) quoted from a Canadian Bank of Commerce letter dated March 2, 1958. I think it is interesting that the hon. member should have quoted from that bank letter, because in my research I found-though it is possible that I may not be correct-that the first Canadian branch bank to be opened in the West Indies was established by the Canadian Bank of Commerce in 1889. I have quoted figures which show a decrease in Canadian participation in the wheat flour market of the West Indies. But statistics also show that Canada still continues to be a better customer of the West Indies than the United States. It has been

mentioned in the course of this debate that we give a preference of $1 on sugar, whereas I understand the United States does all it can to keep that sugar out. I point out to hon. gentlemen opposite, that good intentions alone will not give us this market. If it did, then I say we would have a bigger proportion of the Canadian wheat flour market because, according to my figures, we have maintained a better and larger ratio of imports from the West Indies than has the United States.
I have been disappointed in the debate on this point. The debate has been brought forward in a rather mild form of generalization by the hon. member who presented the resolution. Nowhere in the debate has any indication been given as to what would be the attitude of the West Indies toward a proposal of free trade with Canada. Surely to goodness if this resolution means all that it says it does it should be based on the benefits that accrue which would be mutually shared by both parties. Nowhere in the debate has this been mentioned.
There was much meat in the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twill-ingate. We have a new federation within the commonwealth bestirring itself, seeking to be established and coming to the fore. This opens a great vista in the opinion of those of us who believe in trade. I am sure that is the view of all hon. members without regard to political affiliation and I am sure it is the desire of all of us to take the greatest possible advantage of it. I am sure this cannot be done by this government alone nor can it be done by any government alone. To take the fullest advantage of it will require the complete co-operation of government, business, and indeed all individuals and producers alike.
I do not wish to prolong the debate and I have no further information to place on the record but before winding up my short presentation I wish to comment on one thing that was said by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) who proposed the resolution which rather struck my fancy. I do not know if in fact anything can be perfect but the hon. gentleman said that this resolution is politically perfectly timed. We are about to witness the birth of a new federation within the commonwealth and if the hon. member had gone a little further I would say that I completely agree with his remark that the resolution is politically perfectly timed because today we have in power on the treasury benches a government which is dedicated to expanding trade. We have a Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) who is ever watchful and eager to seize any proper opportunity to expand Canada's trade. I know that we can depend on him to bring forward

a policy that will benefit not only Canada but the Federation of the West Indies, soon to be a new member of the commonwealth.
To that degree and with that qualification I agree fully with the proposer of this resolution and it would have my support if he had phrased it a little differently. But I am suspicious of this resolution being proposed on the subject of free trade by a member of the party to which the hon. member for Ottawa West belongs. If he had proposed that this government be alert and use its efforts for expanding trade between Canada and the West Indies I could support the resolution 100 per cent.
