speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to tell you that it is with some misgivings that I rise to speak in this house. Having been elected for the first time on March 31st last, I know that I am necessarily lacking in experience but the wish to serve the voters of my riding of Laval, who put their trust in me, is giving me the confidence any representative of the people has to feel to remain worthy of the name.
Mr. Speaker, the matter now before us must be of interest to all Canadians. Indeed, trade with another country is considered an important part of our economy, and I believe it is not too soon to say to hon. members that I am in favour of free trade with that country, if we take essential precautions for the protection of both nations.
However, before proceeding any further, I should like, if I may, recall briefly the historical background of the trade agreements between Canada and the West Indies. I read this from an article which appeared in Foreign Trade, a fortnightly publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce. In this issue of January 4, 1958, Miss M. V. McCormick, of the international trades relation branch writes as follows:
Canada has a long history of trade with the West Indies, stretching back well over 200 years. We
Canada-West Indies Trade have sold them principally flour, fish, other foodstuffs, and lumber:	they have sold us sugar,
molasses, lumber, spices and tropical fruits. In recent years the trade has taken on a more varied complexion: bauxite, alumina and petroleum have been coming to us from the West Indies and we have been sending them a wide variety of manufactured goods.
In the last twenty years this trade has grown in size as well as in scope. Just before the Second World War the total trade with the West Indies, both imports and exports, reached $33 million. By 1956, it had increased to $113 million, with our exports to the West Indies totalling $49 million and our imports from the islands $64 million. Figures for the first nine months of 1957 show exports to the West Indies at $35 million and imports from the West Indies for the first six months of 1957 at $40 million, a substantial rise over the 1956 figure.
The close trading relations between Canada and the British West Indies over the years are the result of several factors. The economies of the two areas are largely complementary and the areas themselves are not far apart, geographically speaking. In addition, three successive trade agreements have provided a framework for the building-up of this trade.
At the turn of the century, the British West Indies lost its sugar market in the United States and became interested in the possibility of selling sugar in Canada instead. At that time, total Canada-B.W.I. trade had an annual value of less than $5 million and both sides wanted to increase it. This feeling, plus the desire for Empire solidarity within the Imperial Preferential Tariff system, paved the way for the first Canada-West Indies Trade Agreement of 1912.
The 1912 agreement gave Canada preferential rates of duty of four-fifths of the general tariff on specified goods and provided that some British West Indian products, notably sugar, would receive corresponding preferential treatment in Canada. In 1920, this agreement was replaced by a broader one under which preferences applied to all dutiable goods on both sides, with a few exceptions. Canada gave the British West Indies a tariff preference of 50 per cent on all dutiable articles other than tobacco, cigars, cigarettes and spirituous or alcoholic liquors.
A third and more extensive trade agreement, the one now in force, was signed on July 6, 1925, and came into operation on April 30, 1927. This agreement broadened the exchange of preferences still further and made various special provisions for individual products and for individual colonies. It provided that import duties on Canadian products may not exceed certain percentages of the mostfavoured-nation rates. These percentages vary in different colonies:	for example, they may not
exceed 50 per cent in Barbados, British Guiana and Trinidad, or 75 per cent in Jamaica. For a few other products-notably flour, dairy products, meat, fish, apples, potatoes and alcoholic beverages- specified margins of preference that were set forth in the agreement were granted to imports from Canada. In fact, virtually every product imported from Canada received some tariff preference.
For its part, Canada granted free entry to a number of British West Indian products and consolidated margins of preference on most dutiable imports, including sugar. The most important preference was that on raw sugar when im-

Canada-West Indies Trade
ported by refiners for refining in Canada. The bound margin of preference on 96-degree sugar was increased to $1.00 per 100 pounds under the 1927 agreement, and other raw sugar imported by refiners received equivalent preferential treatment. Other important products on which Canada granted preferences were bananas, cocoa beans, rum, coffee and spices. In addition, Canada gave a general undertaking that the duty on all goods imported from the West Indies but not specifically enumerated in the agreement would at no time exceed 50 per cent of the general tariff of Canada.
This agreement was to remain in force for twelve years. However, because of the war it was renewed in 1939 for an indefinite period. It may be terminated on six months' notice.
As we can see, Mr. Speaker, the trade situation between Canada and the British West Indies is not too bad. On the other hand, I say that there is room for improvement and that Canada could find profit in intensifying this trade.
In the same publication, Mr. Rex Stoll-meyer, trade commissioner for the British West Indies, British Guiana and British Honduras, in Montreal, writes this:
The hope that Canadians will avail themselves of investment opportunities and incentives in the British West Indies is based on three factors. In the first place, Canadian investment will contribute to Caribbean development and this in turn will increase trade and West Indian purchases of Canadian exports. Second, investment in the West Indies has particular advantages for Canadians. Hitherto investment in the small, fragmentary markets has not been attractive. Under customs union and free trade conditions in the next few years a British Caribbean market of three million will emerge, a circumstance which is already stimulating investment interest. Branch plants in the Carribbean could serve as bases for distribution within the area and to the adjacent Latin American countries. More important, plants established in these soft currency territories could serve other commonwealth areas without encountering the currency problems faced by home-based Canadian exporters. Another approach would be for semi-finished products to be sent to plants in the area for the final stages of manufacture.
Secondly, the tourist potentialities of the area are far from fully developed and in some territories are almost completely unexploited.
Finally, there is a persistent and considerable amount of Canadian interest in the British West Indies which has always lent grace to the trading relationship. The West Indies hopes soon to be the second Dominion in the New World, a development which ought to lead to a maturing of this long-established and reciprocated sentiment. Much has been said about the complementary nature of the two economies from the point of view of both trade and investment. Nothing could be more conducive to Canada-West Indies solidarity than that trade between the two areas should grow. This will require greater West Indian purchasing power through development. And Canada could contribute to that development through sustained imports from the area, an inflow of tourists, and the injection of investment capital in industrial development and the tourist trade.
However, before explaining the part played by Canadian capital in trade with the British

West Indies, Mr. Stollmeyer had carefully recommended the following encouragement to investments:
Over-riding requirements for a viable West Indian economy (itself a prerequisite for autonomy) are capital and know-how. Currently the territories are making efforts of varying degrees of intensity to improve their agriculture, to encourage industrial development, and to stimulate the tourist trade. In the two latter fields, greater attention is being given to attracting capital from overseas. Several inducements are being offered to investors in industry. All the territories allow new or underdeveloped industries periods of freedom from income tax ranging from five to seven years, with duty-free import of plant, equipment and machinery for such "pioneer industries". In addition, some territories, notably Trinidad, offer special rates of depreciation following the "tax holiday"; these are calculated to ease the impact of income tax. Jamaica goes farther, with an Export Industry Encouragement Law which affords duty-free entry of raw materials in addition to the usual income tax and duty concessions to companies manufacturing solely for export. An International Business Companies Law provides perpetual freedom from income tax for business companies not trading in the British West Indies, British Guiana and British Honduras.
The tourist industry has become a major source of revenue, and particularly of dollars, for the British West Indies as a result of the great number of Canadians and Americans visiting the islands. Prospects for expansion are excellent. Promotion programs are constantly under way to increase the flow of tourists throughout the year. The tourist interests of all the territories are represented by the office of the trade commissioner in Montreal -with the exception of British Guiana, which has separate representation, and Jamaica, which maintains a tourist bureau in Toronto.
Recent years have brought great pressure on resort facilities in the British West Indies. Local investment in tourist accommodation has increased and considerable overseas capital has come into Jamaica and, to a somewhat lesser degree, into Barbados and Trinidad. The pace of investment in the area as a whole, however, has not been quick enough and some of the territories have passed incentive legislation aimed at encouraging it. Generally speaking, this legislation offers freedom from income tax during initial stages of operation, plus freedom from import duty on capital equipment. Three territories-British Guiana, Jamaica and Trinidad-publish attractive booklets describing development conditions and outlining inducements for investment in industry and the tourist trade.
Mr. Speaker, those are a few opinions I have gathered from authorities on the matter we are considering. I feel that if we read this material it will help us give better and fuller consideration to the matter of trade with the British West Indies in order that the greatest possible number of Canadians may benefit from this market which, in the long run, will prove very interesting for the whole of Canada.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
In rising on this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I am mindful, as have been the other members who spoke here this afternoon, of how important is our trade with the West Indies. In 1957 it provided the second largest market Canada had in the British commonwealth of nations, surpassed only by our exports to the United Kingdom. In 1956 we sold $49 million worth of products in the West Indies. In 1957 our export trade totalled over $61 million. This market is all the more important when it is recalled that about 85 per cent of the goods that Canada sells in the West Indies can be classed as manufactured or semimanufactured. By comparison only 15 per cent to 20 per cent of the goods we sell to the United Kingdom are manufactured or semi-manufactured. As an example, we sell wheat to the United Kingdom, whereas we sell flour to the West Indies. About 10 per cent of all Canadian flour finds a market there. Other manufactured goods that we sell to the federation consist of boots and shoes, paint, small furniture, machinery, rubber goods, steel pipes and tubes, fittings and other similar products.
Many of our products which we find it more difficult to sell in the more highly developed parts of the world are able to find a market in the British West Indies because these islands are not yet industrialized and they are not attempting, so much as other countries, to protect home industries. Our trade with the West Indies is very important to every part of Canada. The west coast sells lumber and canned salmon; the prairies sell flour; Ontario and Quebec sell a large variety of manufactured goods. But the participation of so many maritime members in this debate today, is evidence of how important the Atlantic provinces regard this market. We, in the eastern provinces, think it holds a special attraction for us. At the moment we sell a large quantity of fish in the West Indies. Our sales have increased from about $900,000 in 1937, to $3.5 million in 1947 and to $6.1 million in 1955. We also find a market there for apples, potatoes and other foodstuffs, and for some manufactured products such as boots and shoes. We hope to be able to increase our sales and our present exports to the West Indies of these non-manufactured goods.
However, the great prospect so far as we are concerned of this West Indian market is a sale for manufactured goods as maritime industry expands. As hon. members all know,
Canada-West Indies Trade the chief problem that faces the Atlantic provinces today is the problem of industrialization. We must manufacture goods in our provinces, to provide employment there and to increase the gross product of our provinces. Before confederation, the Atlantic provinces could sell in two directions. They could sell to the people in the West Indies and to the cities of the United States; and, they could sell up the St. Lawrence to Ontario and Quebec. Indeed, prior to confederation we enjoyed a very favourable geographical position astride the main shipping lanes and water routes from Montreal and Quebec, to eastern United States cities and to the ports of the West Indies. The ports of Halifax and Saint John and Louisburg were midway ports where sailing ships could stop to be refitted and supplied. This was a very important trade in the early days of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
Then, suddenly the east-west traffic that developed as a result of confederation cut off the advantage of the maritimes in this traffic between eastern United States and West Indian ports and Ontario and Quebec. When manufacturing capital came into Canada it came into the central provinces for the very simple reason that the more central location made it possible for factories there to sell east and west. At the same time the factories in the maritimes could not compete with the factories on the scene in Ontario and Quebec. Of course, the transportation edge that the central provinces had, meant the decline of industries that flourished in the maritimes before confederation, and an ever increasing lack of opportunity.
Any manufacturer who wishes to establish an industry, must first of all look to his local and domestic market to build up primary sales which are his "bread and butter". If he has a good local market where he is sheltered his primary profits at home will build up his capital and establish him. Then after his industry has had a chance to root he can look for wider markets in other areas to increase his profits. Our problem in the Atlantic provinces has been that we do not have a sufficient local market to allow our infant industries to root. They must, from the first, enter into the highly competitive Ontario-Quebec market.
In terms of this geographical situation the possibility of a market in the West Indies is a very interesting prospect for the Atlantic provinces. We are 1,000 miles closer to the West Indies markets than are the factories in the Montreal area; about 1,200 miles closer

Canada-West Indies Trade than the factories in eastern Ontario. We should be able to manufacture and sell goods to the 3.5 million people who live in the British West Indies cheaper than similar goods can be sold by other Canadian factories. We should be able also to bring goods to this market cheaper than they can be brought from the United Kingdom. It is true that the annual income of the people in the West Indies is not high. This market can absorb only a limited quantity of Canadian goods from any area. Nevertheless, added to the population of the Atlantic provinces, the 3.5 million people in this federation will greatly increase our chance of a sufficiently sheltered primary market to give industries in the eastern provinces an opportunity to develop.
It is certainly to the advantage of our Atlantic provinces in particular that Canada should develop trade with the West Indies federation, and that these islands should prosper and increase in wealth. It is obvious that Canada would be unable to compete in this West Indian market at all if it were not for the preferential tariff that we enjoy. United States factories can produce cheaper. They are closer, and without the preferential tariff assistance we could not place goods to any considerable degree in this West Indian market. Even now the value of the goods we sell there does not approximate what is being sold by United States industries. Every year the United States sells the islands considerably more manufactured goods than we do, despite our preferential tariff.
Our goods do find a market in the West Indies, because we have this preferential agreement and simply because we buy more goods from the West Indies than does the United States. Nearly 80 per cent of the exports of Barbados and 40 per cent of the exports of Jamaica consist of sugar and molasses. About 70 per cent of these products is purchased by the United Kingdom, and a large amount of the remaining 30 per cent is purchased by Canada.
Since 1903 the United States has given special tariff preference to Cuba, the Phil-lipines, Puerto Rico and Hawaii. When the West Indies were denied an American sugar market, they turned to Canada. Our trade with the Caribbean countries has stemmed from the fact that we have purchased their sugar. In recent years, of course, the discovery of bauxite deposits in British Guiana and later in Jamaica, from which most or a large part of the aluminum that is produced in Canada is made, greatly increased our trade with the West Indies.
There can be no question that we can greatly increase our exports to the British West Indies if we give proper care and attention to this market. In 1947 we sold
[Mr. MacLellan.l
$61 million worth of products in the British West Indies. By 1950 the value of our exports had fallen sharply to $21 million. The figure has been improving steadily since then but still at $51 million, it is far from the amount that we sold to the British West Indies in 1947. We should be able to improve our export position in the British West Indies very substantially yet.
Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree, as is proposed by the resolution, that we should eliminate or at least decrease our tariff with the British West Indies as a method of expanding our trade in that area. While I support the resolution, I am aware that there are great obstacles to its fulfilment. One of the difficulties, as has been mentioned, is the fact that the federation has not yet achieved a tariff agreement or a customs union and each of the islands still has its own customs system. To do business with the federation on that basis would be very difficult. The commission on trade and tariffs set up under the chairmanship of Sir William Croft has not yet submitted its findings as a result of its inquiry into the tariff and customs problems of the area. No doubt any move towards free trade with these islands would have to await the adoption of that report and the accomplishment of a customs union among the islands.
I also realize, Mr. Speaker, that it is doubtful that the islands or the British West Indies federation could remove all tariffs. As we all know these islands, like many other undeveloped areas, do not have the same tax sources to rely upon as we have. There is no substantial income tax possibility in the British West Indies and an important part of the revenue of each of the governments that administrates these islands is from tariffs and customs. It is very doubtful if they or even the federation could agree to eliminate all tariffs since such a large part of the revenue of the federation, as formerly to the governments of the islands, comes from tariffs and customs duties.
There is another very serious consideration as far as we are concerned, Mr. Speaker, that I recognize will have to be faced if this resolution were adopted. I refer to the fact that further or more complete free trade or a more complete trade union with the British West Indies federation could imperil other important markets we have in the Caribbean area. We have in Cuba and in other countries in that area important markets which we could possibly lose if we entered into an agreement with the British West Indies which made it too difficult for these other countries to sell to us. These markets, have to some extent been much

more important to us than the British West Indies market. For example, while our fish exports to the British West Indies are important, we cannot afford to have our markets in the other islands there cut ofE.
In the three years from 1954 to 1956 our average fish sales in the Caribbean area totalled $14,096,000. Of this amount 62 per cent found markets in non-British Caribbean countries, while only 38 per cent was sold to the British West Indies. It can easily be seen that the 62 per cent we sell to nonBritish countries is too important a market as far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned for us to take any risk of losing it or impeding it. Furthermore, our market in the non-British West Indies is oftentimes more lucrative than is our market in the British West Indies. As hon. members all know, over the last few years our sales of salt fish in the British West Indies have not been as lucrative as they could be or as they have been in non-British countries. The whole matter will have to receive serious study. I say, of course, that I support the resolution and that the matter of freer trade with the British West Indies is important not only to the Atlantic provinces but to all of Canada.
There is another thing that we must face with regard to trade with the West Indies. It is not simply a matter of our reducing or eliminating tariffs to see our trade suddenly increased tenfold with the British West Indies. The simple fact is that if we are going to have a larger trade with these islands we must be prepared to buy more from them. At the moment the chief disadvantage to trading with the islands is not so much tariffs as it is quotas limiting our sales to them. The islands' purchases of our products must be limited by our purchases from them. Despite the preferential tariff that we have, Canadian goods going into the West Indies meet a quota system that puts an arbitrary limit on the amount of goods that we can sell there. The only way in which we can conquer that difficulty is to assist the West Indies to find a larger market for goods in Canada.
In the case of molasses, ginger, nutmegs, lime juice and arrowroot, the colonies now sell to about half the Canadian market. They have half the market in regard to these products. But they supply only 10 per cent of our cocoa and less than 1 per cent of our coffee. We could greatly increase our purchases of coffee and cocoa, and of course we could greatly increase our purchases of bananas and citrus fruits. Prior to 1939 we bought half of our bananas from the British West Indies. The war, hurricanes and plant disease brought this trade to an end. Since
Canada-West Indies Trade the war, producers in Central America have captured the market here and efforts to reintroduce Jamaican bananas have been unsuccessful. The simple fact is that the large banana market that the West Indies once had in Canada was lost and the producers of bananas in that area do not now have the funds or the ability with which to build up in Canada a distribution system that could sell their bananas here. No matter how much we should like to help them in that regard, their products have to be warehoused and sold to the wholesaler and of course ultimately to the consumers. At the moment the banana market in Canada is tied up by a large United States complex that produces this product in Central America, and it would be quite a problem for the West Indies federation to increase its market in Canada for this very important product of the islands.
Mr. Speaker, over the last 200 years our trade and our relations with the British West Indies have been very important to Canada. We in the Atlantic provinces in particular are tied to them with friendly memories that are as old as the settlement of the Atlantic provinces and as old as the cities of the east. Our economies are not competitive. The products that they grow, such as citrus fruits and fruits of the tropical variety, are not products that we can grow here. We can provide a market here, if we wish to do so, for the products of the West Indies. At the same time the products that we grow in this temperate climate in Canada are not such as can be grown in the British West Indies. We should be able to find a greatly increased market there for products which they do not grow well and which are not indigenous to that climate. We should be able to increase our sales of potatoes, beef and many other similar products in the Caribbean area but it is most important that we should not think the only thing we need to do in order to increase our sales to the West Indies federation is to decrease or eliminate our tariffs.
The tariff is only a very small part of the problem. Before we can enter into a free trade relationship or greatly increase our trade with the federation it must have a chance to settle down, to form its customs union and to gain strength as a nation. A federation formed this year can hardly be expected all at once to achieve a solution to all the internal problems which it faces, many of which are an impediment to its trade with the outside world, particularly with Canada. We must wait, therefore, for many of these problems to be overcome.

Canada-West Indies Trade
The trade carried on between the West Indies and Britain is very vital to the federation. The grants and aid of the United Kingdom over the years have kept the island governments in revenue. We cannot expect to cut too sharply into the extensive trade between the islands and the United Kingdom until the federation has reached a point where it is more self-sufficient. Certainly I support this resolution and I feel it is greatly in the interests of Canada generally and in the interests of my part of the country in particular to see trade fostered and increased in that area. We should assist the new federation in any way we can and by so doing I believe we will be making a great investment for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the taller member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) has already taken part in this debate and I have no wish therefore, on the short end of the Tory ticket, to defer the consideration by the house of the resolution before us. There are, however, two observations I wish to make which I will illustrate with some factual material from one industry which I know has captivated the attention of many hon. members today. I have in mind the fisheries industry.
It seems to me that while the resolution in its present wording is attractive, here is a field in which we should make haste slowly. The institution of free trade cannot, alas, be brought about by resolutions and as the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan) has just pointed out, there are sizeable obstacles in the way of this particular resolution, primarily having to do with matters of currency but also with respect to the present negotiations within the West Indies for its own customs union. *Without any finality in this respect we cannot anticipate an early or an agreeable settlement of the trade problems which exist between this country and the West Indies.
There are also important problems concerning the several branches of Canadian industry which are not supplementary to West Indies industry and which should be carefully considered before we advance too hasitly into something which may look at the moment and may in time prove to be attractive, but which at present has in its way many difficulties.
We on this side of the house are mindful of the fact that one of the surest tests of friendship-as we were reminded the other day in this very house by the President of the United States-is the capacity to speak frankly. While free trade between Canada and the West Indies may be desirable as a goal it ought not to be overlooked that there


are problems to solve and if we intend to provide for the people of the West Indies that comradeship in the British tradition which they seek in a divided world and for which they have looked in the first instance to Canada, then we ought to be able to deal frankly and candidly with them in respect of our present trading problems.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate (Mr. Pickersgill) in a very informative speech this evening mentioned many other matters including the desirability of a federal subsidy-if I understood him correctly- which would equalize the shipping costs on Newfoundland salt fish with that of Nova Scotia.

speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman must have misunderstood me. I did not suggest a subsidy for that purpose at all; I did suggest that if Canadian National steamships could be operated from Halifax and St. John's as well then presumably the rate would be equalized.

Yes, of course it did. I am sorry and I understand the clarification now made. However, the hon. member will agree that this matter of subsidies has been presented before, indeed recently in the other place, and I would like to refer to the St. John's Telegram of July 2, a newspaper with which I am sure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is fully familiar, which quoted a political friend of his as having said in the other place that a federal subsidy is, in effect, desirable in order to equalize shipping costs. It is upon that point, in any event, which I wish to dwell at this moment.
I do not think it is widely understood that the matter of federal subsidies came up several times while the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships were operating. The equalization of freight rates from St. John's and Halifax to the Caribbean market might be a serious blow to Nova Scotia fish exporters and we would like to have this borne in mind with respect to consideration of future trade relationships between the two areas. It is, for instance, true that about 75 per cent, or perhaps more, of the salt fish we now process in Nova Scotia and export to the Caribbean actually originates in Newfoundland in its salt bulk state. This fish is brought into Nova Scotia as salt bulk fish at a very substantial freight cost to our exporters and, what is more, freight is required to be paid on each 165 pounds of wet produce which

ultimately comes down to 100 pounds of dried fish. This great cost is an additional expenditure borne by the Nova Scotia salt fish dealer, so that we have a higher freight rate than Newfoundland has in respect of shipments of dried salt cod to the Caribbean, that is, higher via Halifax. Therefore equalization of freight rates such as suggested in the other place would, we think, put our Nova Scotia exporters or could put them at a very serious disadvantage in competing on fish sales to the Caribbean.
I do not think it is widely understood, furthermore, that the people of the West Indies are not the largest importers of Canadian fish in the Caribbean area. Perhaps the erroneous impression has been given this afternoon that the West Indies are Canada's most important salt and pickled fish market. The British West Indies are not Canada's most important salt and pickled fish market. That is, not in the Caribbean. In all, the non-British West Indies market takes about 60 per cent of Canada's salt and pickled dried fish.

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman means "non-British" does he not?

maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
I was just coming to that point. The non-British takes 60 per cent and the British portion takes only 40 per cent. That is, the percentage of our exports going to the British West Indies territories in the Caribbean is 40 per cent. Without taking into account the higher per capita earnings of the consumers and the higher standard of living in the various countries of the British West Indies or, if you wish, the entire Caribbean area, the combined population of the British West Indies is between three million and three and a half million. But the combined population of Cuba, Haiti, Puerto Rico, Panama and the Dominican Republic is over 15 million, and in advocating free trade with the British West Indies we should have regard to the fact that the total consumer population there is only one-fifth of the population of the non-British part of the Caribbean. Jamaica has traditionally been the largest of the British West Indian markets, with imports in the area of 17 million pounds of salt cod annually, and it is upon this point that I wish to dwell for a moment.
This Jamaican market involves a consumer price ceiling at the present time; a consumer price ceiling which, as far as the Canadian fisherman is concerned, prevents the normal laws of supply and demand from functioning. For instance, at this moment, while we are debating here, mackerel is in short supply on the Canadian east coast. Yet the Jamaican market, by imposing a consumer price ceiling, prevents the normal play
Canada-West Indies Trade of the law of supply and demand, and, in effect, deprives Canadian fishermen of the price increase which they would normally expect to result from the short supply reaching the market. This consumer price ceiling on the Canadian salt cod is a hand-down, a carry-over from the second world war, but it still exists; the price ceiling in Jamaica, has in fact, in recent months been lower than it was four or five years ago, so the law of supply and demand does not operate fully, and for years Canadian fishermen have not been able, when exporting to this consumer price ceiling market, to take normal advantage of short supplies. In addition, there was a single price for all five sizes of the product which we export.
Mr. Speaker, in assessing the desirability of moving toward a free trade complex with the West Indies I should like to suggest to the government that consideration be given to the fact that some hon. members feel that the maintenance of these price ceilings is not entirely compatible with the present preferential trade advantage which we give to such countries as Jamaica, for instance. We find, for example, that under the Canada-British West Indies trade agreement the Canadian import duty on raw sugar imported from Jamaica is now 28 cents per 100 pounds as compared with $1.28 per hundred pounds on sugar exported to Canada from such countries as Cuba and the Dominican Republic. I suggest that hon. members from Nova Scotia representing fishing groups such as exist in my own large constituency may well feel that granting this preferential trade, which I am sure is a desirable thing in the eyes of the mover of this resolution, to the British West Indies producers has in fact led to the curtailment of the sales of our Canadian salt and pickled fish in the Jamaican market. In 1926, before the Canada-British West Indies treaty was proclaimed, Canadian fish entered Cuba, for instance, at a duty of $1.30 per 100 kilos. In 1930, I find, Cuba raised the duty to $3 and increased it again two years later to $5.50. The rate of duty today is $4 per 100 kilos.
I should like to suggest to the government and to the minister who will be most concerned with this resolution before us that in considering what has been said here today he should take into account that if there is to be a continuation of preferential trade, or an expansion of it; if there is to be a continuation of the present tariff preferences by Canada to the West Indies, that these tariff preferences be bargained against the elimination of or the reduction in the number of consumer price ceilings on the product which we try to export. We think that there are

Canada-West Indies Trade discriminatory restrictive controls on the import into Jamaica of certain Canadian products. I have in mind, especially, the Jamaican ceiling on salt cod. And I believe it is true that instead of there being any widespread indication of a change in the attitude of the Jamaican government in regard to this matter, the government of Jamaica did in fact negotiate this year, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate well knows, for the purchase of 3,000 tons of salt cod from Iceland, and this after years of preferential treatment in our markets. This is a considerable amount, more than one-third of the normal importation of salt cod in Jamaica.
Some of us feel that it is not unreasonable to ask the government to consider, in extending preferential trade agreements or in continuing them in their present form, and having regard to the traditions of British fair play and British friendship and candour, to consider the fact that sometimes these preferential trade arrangements as steps along the way to free trade sometimes do not work out in practice as the words in the resolution suggest they will.
The association of fish dealers in Nova Scotia has computed that in 1956, the last year for which comparable statistics in all fields of trade were available, the total dollar value of all the salt and pickled fish that we Canadians sold in the Jamaican market alone ran to about $3,250,000. By virtue of the sugar preference alone, the Jamaican sugar industry received in preferential treatment what amounts to a figure over $2,500,000. That is more than would have been realized if, for instance, the $1 per 100 pounds preference had not existed; that is, if it had been eliminated entirely. One could say, expressing it another way,-although this probably suffers some of the exaggeration of brevity- that the Canadian government would have been worse off only to the extent of about $350,000 in that full calendar year 1956 if it had donated the salted and pickled fish that Jamaica purchased from Canada instead of giving the sugar preference at all. So that preferential trade has not always worked to the full advantage of the Canadian industry.
Nothing that I have said in giving this as one illustration is intended in any way to diminish the placidity with which this debate has been conducted today. It has been free of partisan rancour. We have all tried to give expression to what is foremost in our minds and that is the good of the people whom we were sent here to represent in the first place, and the good of all Canadians, in the second. If I have made any point at all it is the simple one of using the argument of the impact of trading relationships upon the industry in

my area; indeed the desirability in these matters of making haste slowly.
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) that at some future time when he is considering the complex of trade delegations to markets as important to hon. members on all sides of the house as is Jamaica-which I understand according to the press a trade delegation may visit next February-

speakeroldname: Mr. M. J. A. Lambert (Edmonton West):
maintopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF FREE TRADE BETWEEN CANADA AND THE WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we have heard speakers mostly from the eastern regions of Canada and perhaps hon. members would wonder why a member from western Canada should rise to speak on this particular subject. In reply to that question I would say that coming from a surplus producing region of this country-like hon. members from various other sections of western Canada-we have an inclination toward free trade or trade that is as free as possible because we fully realize that if we are to dispose of our surplus products we would prefer having not to contend with any artificial barriers, or as few as possible of these.
The resolution before us this evening strikes me as being rather premature and while I perhaps fully apprehend the motives of the hon. member who proposed the resolution I am wondering whether he has achieved his true intention, whether he wanted free trade with the Federation of the West Indies. I would have thought that the hon. member would have recognized that in the foreseeable future and until world economic and sociological conditions change such a goal would be unattainable.
There are certainly some very practical obstacles to free trade with the Federation of the West Indies and indeed with many other countries although we would perhaps be governed by the particular trading position we were in when deciding about the desirability of free trade of this kind. First of all there is the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. Since we are tied in with many other Carribean countries-as is the United States which in particular has extensive interests in Central America and the Caribbean region-we could not possibly enter a free trade agreement without very wide and sweeping amendments to the GATT. I would suggest that at this time the obstacles would be insurmountable.
Then, too, the matter of free trade is not something that can be imposed by one country on another. Perhaps we would be prepared to consider free trade but we must first know what is the position of the Federation of the West Indies in this connection. They are possibly the newest entity in the commonwealth but so new are they that they have not even worked out a free trade arrangement among themselves. Before free trade between Canada and the West Indies
Canada-West Indies Trade would be possible, I suggest that they would require to have their domestic situation sorted out. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that their own problems will not be solved tomorrow.
I agree that there is a field in which Canadian trade can be developed to a considerable extent in the future, but until they are prepared to deal with us how can we be in a position to enter into such an agreement as is proposed by this resolution? They would have to work out a customs union amongst themselves or do as we do here in Canada where we have at least nominally free trade among the provinces. I would suggest that there may be some obstacles to interprovincial trade but our constitution says that there should not be. However, that is not too apparent in some cases.
Then, there is another difficulty. The West Indies federation operates within the sterling bloc, and that presents an immediate problem. The federation is not the master of its own ship in matters of its currency convertibility. We are dealing at the present time, in so far as the West Indies are concerned, with quantity restrictions. Imports from Canada are limited by quantity restrictions.
However, it is interesting to look at the trade statistics for 1957. We find that those colonies within the commonwealth, which now make up the Federation of the West Indies, sold goods to Canada to the total value of a little over $58 million in 1957, but we sold to them only $40 million worth. Since we are considering this matter, I would say that a number of members and quite a few of the Canadian public, along with myself, were rather surprised at those figures. They would have believed-I certainly assumed it before I made my investigation-that we had sold a great deal more to the federation than we imported from them, but such was not the case. Our greatest single import, of course, is aluminum bauxite from Jamaica. Then we have sugar and sugar products, particularly raw sugar.
To get back to what benefit would result in greater trade with the West Indies, or what benefit could be derived from greater trade with the Federation of the West Indies, in addition to the untold quantities of fish of which we have heard a good deal this afternoon and this evening, they could absorb agricultural products from western Canada in the form of flour particularly and perhaps meats. With the advent of the St. Lawrence seaway and a lower cost on the transportation of wheat I believe that we could certainly compete advantageously in the West Indies market with our flour. However, there we have certain competition from our friends across the line who in latter years have

Canada-West Indies Trade shown that they too consider this to be an opportune market and they are prepared to be very competitive about it.
We in western Canada find ourselves at the greatest possible distance from the source of citrus fruits. I had always wondered why it was necessary to buy most of our citrus fruits from California, Texas, Louisiana and Florida, and why we did not see any from the West Indies. I am told-and here I am merely going on hearsay-that there is a question of quality control; that naturally as far as western Canada is concerned the cost of transportation of certain types of citrus fruits would be high. However, with the improvement in refrigeration and the possibilities of bringing in cargoes of fresh fruit under refrigerated conditions to the lake-head and then by rail to the various markets of western Canada, I think there is an opportunity there. However, that is to come in the future.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, what I suspect is that the aim of the hon. member who proposed this resolution is not so much free trade with the Federation of the West Indies as the expansion of trade with that federation. I believe all hon. members and the Canadian public would be prepared to go along with him, but the question of free trade, as I have indicated, is entirely something that is so far away as to be completely impracticable. As the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris) pointed out a few minutes ago, the small proportion of the population of the federation compared to the whole Caribbean area would, I suggest, create very grave problems in our trade relations with other areas such as the countries of South America which border on the Caribbean, and the Central America states to whom we sell and from whom we buy a lot.

maintopic: MEMBERS OF THE SENATE AND OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS CHAMBER, OTTAWA, ON MONDAY, JULY 21, 1958, AT 11 A.M.

speechtext: Dr. Nkrumah was welcomed by the Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker, Prime Minister of Canada, and thanked by the Hon. Mark Robert Drouin, Speaker of the Senate, and the Hon. Roland Michener, Speaker of the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister of Canada):
maintopic: MEMBERS OF THE SENATE AND OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS CHAMBER, OTTAWA, ON MONDAY, JULY 21, 1958, AT 11 A.M.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker of the Senate, Mr. Speaker of the House of Commons, and members of the parliament of Canada: Dr. Nkrumah, on behalf of the parliament and people of Canada I extend a warm welcome to you and your ministers who are associated with you on this occasion, Hon. Mr. Botsio and Hon. Mr. Baako. I welcome you as the prime minister of the first truly African state to attain dominion status within the commonwealth.
I first met Dr. Nkrumah at the prime ministers' conference in London last June, a few short months after his country had become an independent nation within the commonwealth. I think the emergence of Ghana to equal status within the commonwealth is symbolic of the commonwealth concept as it develops to meet change and changing conditions. Canadians have pride in the role that Canada has played in the evolution of this commonwealth. In this commonwealth, nations, equal and independent, join together in their dedication to freedom through the practice of parliamentary democracy in the tradition of the mother of parliaments at Westminster, thereby bringing peace, progress and prosperity to peoples everywhere in the world.
It was Sir Robert Borden who in 1919, following the sacrifices of the first world war, secured for Canada recognition of her sovereign status as a signatory of the peace treaty and as a member of the league of nations; further steps along that pathway have been taken by succeeding prime ministers of Canada. The commonwealth to me represents an institution which, in its inherent greatness, gives hope to mankind. A world organization of many races, beliefs and religions, we have no political uniformity without law or by law; its unity is in the dedication of its peoples to freedom; its glory
is that all share in a common heritage; its purpose, peace for all mankind; the bonds of its unity maintained by the good sense, good will and good faith of its diverse peoples.
Because of this principle it does not stagnate in formalism. It is ever growing; it is living. From time to time in the years ahead other nations will join its ranks and two confederations, that of Nigeria and that of the West Indies, have not long to wait for membership.
If I might I should like to say a word as to the constitution of Ghana, for it illustrates what I have placed before you, namely that there is no uniformity in the political systems of the various portions of this commonwealth. Ghana has a unicameral legislature. Five regions comprise the state which came about through the uniting of the Gold Coast with Togoland. Each region has an assembly with powers which are not unlike those of our provinces. Each region has a House of Chiefs with power to consider any matter referred to it by a minister or the national assembly.
Mr. Prime Minister, the achievement of full self-governing membership in the commonwealth to which you led your people was a swift, orderly and constitutional march, a tribute to your devotion and a credit to the United Kingdom, which in its finest and best traditions paved the way for the emergence of your nation as a new nation within this commonwealth. Indeed, in little over half a century the commonwealth concept, adapted to the needs of your country, has brought about the transition of a land of diverse peoples with traditional African culture into a modern state with a new and energetic economic life, whose purpose it is to raise the standards of its people and to develop its resources and the talents of its people.
I betray no state secret, Mr. Prime Minister, when I say that last June and July I was deeply impressed by your ability and by your

personal character, and we became friends. I say that as a foundation necessary to the relationships which prevail as between those of us who have responsibilities in all parts of the commonwealth. We have something in common. We were both born on September 18, though you were born a little bit later than I was.
Your life, sir, is an Alger story. Born in a humble home, educated in your own country, you went abroad in order to widen that education in the United States of America, were graduated from Lincoln University and the University of Pennsylvania, and later attended the London School of Economics. I know your philosophy of life from personal conversation with you. However, I prefer to quote your own words on one occasion when you said this: In truth the burden of my life can be summarized in "The Memoriam" quoted by Cecil Rhodes-"So much to do, so little done".
You have done much. You have much still to do in order to bring about that unity among peoples, without regard to colour or race, which has been your life work. It is thus my pleasure to welcome you to Canada, and as a representative of an older partner of the commonwealth to welcome your country as one of the latest in the family of nations within the commonwealth.
I introduce to you the Prime Minister of Ghana, Dr. Kwame Nkrumah.
Dr. Kwame Nkrumah (Prime Minister of Ghana): Mr. Speaker of the Senate, Mr. Speaker of the House of Commons, Mr. Prime Minister, and hon. members of the parliament of Canada: It is a great pleasure for me to address this august assembly today. I wish to express the gratitude of the people of Ghana and my own appreciation for the honour your Prime Minister and his government have done our country by inviting me to pay this visit to Canada. I wish to thank you very sincerely, Mr. Prime Minister, for the kind words with which you have just welcomed me.
We in Ghana have a strong feeling of pride in our commonwealth membership. I had the privilege of attending the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London last year, when for the first time in history the first African state entered that great and free association of states stretching across the world. The meeting provided an invaluable opportunity for establishing personal relationships with other prime ministers and political leaders, and I am particularly happy that I have been able to renew my friendship with your distinguished Prime Minister, Mr. Diefenbaker, for whom I have had great admiration since my first meeting with him.
Address by Dr. Nkrumah
On attaining our independence we in Ghana chose to become a member of the commonwealth of our own free will. We enjoy the same institutions of parliamentary democracy and the same climate of politics and public morality as the other members. We have the same respect for tradition and the same regard for ceremonial. We place the same value on the human individual and appreciate the dignity of restraint. We accept the sovereignty of law and the sanctity of the pledged word.
The family relationship between members of the commonwealth which we have already experienced and which brings together countries widely differing in race, religion and social background, is an example of international association which we shall always support so long as it continues to be based on sound democratic principles and respect for the sovereignty of the member nations.
Canada is in a sense the founder of the commonwealth, for it was in the conception of a free association between Canada and the mother country that the foundations of the commonwealth were laid. Canada has made a great contribution to the world by the successful working of her institutions, her government, the spectacular development of her national resources, and the constructive initiative taken in international affairs. The spirit of tolerance and mutual confidence among peoples of different racial groups that has evolved in this community is an achievement which is a shining example to all of us. Canada also serves as an invaluable link between the great North American continent and its people and the rest of the world.
We believe that Ghana, as the first truly African state to join the commonwealth, also has a contribution to make to the enrichment of the life of the world community. Just as you in Canada have given the world the benefit of your experience and views arising out of your position on this great continent, so we in Africa hope that we will also be able to contribute our views for the common benefit of the community of nations. We feel that through us and through other African nations a general understanding between the African continent and the various members of the commonwealth will be developed. We realize the great responsibilities that this position imposes on us, but we are ready and prepared to take up the challenge.
Recently we took the initiative in convening a conference of independent African states, a conference which proved to be most successful. I myself have recently returned from a tour of the capitals of the other states which participated in the conference. We are endeavouring to establish among ourselves in Africa a fundamental unity on

Address by Dr. Nkrumah domestic and foreign policy which is, I think, of special significance to the role of the African nations in world affairs. We are determined to work together in the economic and cultural fields, with the object of raising the standard of life of our peoples and making a distinctive African contribution to international discussions and the achievement of world peace. We are determined that through mutual co-operation and collective leadership we free and independent African states shall not only safeguard our hard-won independence but also use all the means available to us to emancipate those of our brethren who are still under colonial rule.
I find nothing incompatible with our effectiveness as a member of the United Nations and the commonwealth in pursuing an African objective and projecting an African personality. On the contrary, I see in it great possibilities for good, because we should be able to bring to our deliberations in the United Nations and the commonwealth a better understanding of the African point of view, and make a distinctive contribution toward reaching acceptable solutions to our many problems.
I should like to take this opportunity to comment on certain aspects of our foreign policy. Basically the policy of our government is one of non-alignment and positive neutrality. I have emphasized on several occasions, however, that this should not be interpreted as a purely negative neutralism. On the contrary, we will always adopt whatever positive policy will do most to safeguard our independence. We have a vested interest in peace, and we will do everything in our power to support the United Nations.
Like many other small countries we have appealed to the great powers to suspend nuclear bomb tests. We pray that progress can be made in achieving some degree of disarmament, thus permitting part of the vast resources now applied to the barren task of producing still more terrible weapons of destruction to be transferred to the constructive and hopeful task of assisting the peoples in the less developed countries to eliminate disease and poverty from their lives.
I have come to Canada at a time when great international tension has been generated by recent developments in the Middle East. The attitude of my government to this situation was made clear in the statement issued on July 16, just before I left. We believe that any attempt to pass judgment on what has happened would at this stage simply heighten tension, and the task now is to secure a workable solution for the future. This, we suggest, could be based on three principles: the substitution of a United Nations force for the American troops now in
Lebanon; the holding of free elections in that country under United Nations supervision, and the subsequent establishment of Lebanon as a free and independent state with a status of neutrality, internationally guaranteed on the analogy of Austria. As to the immediate situation, I am confident that I express the views of the leaders of the other independent African states when I say that all of us pray that the leaders of the great powers will come to an understanding which will spare us, who are not parties to their disputes, and the rest of mankind from the unbelievable horrors of modern war. Today, so it seems to me, the fate of mankind rests in the hands of a few men. I pray that they are fully aware of their vast responsibilities.
May I say how greatly we in Ghana have been impressed and inspired by Canada's record in the field of international affairs in recent years. We feel that common sense, decency and reasonableness have invariably reinforced the admirable attitudes you have taken in the United Nations and the wise counsel which you have contributed to the commonwealth.
One other aspect of our international relations on which I wish to touch is that of economic development. Like any other less developed country, we wish to banish disease, ignorance and poverty from our land. We realize that we can only do this in co-operation with other countries and governments. We are the world's greatest producer of cocoa, but like other one-crop countries we are at the mercy of world prices. As you know, the recession of the last year has already had disastrous political consequences quite apart from its economic effects for several of the governments of those less developed areas.
In our own case I attach the highest importance to increasing the productivity of our agriculture, and to starting the industrialization of our country. The cornerstone of our future development is the successful implementation of our great Volta river project for the production of aluminum. Here again the recession has affected our basic plans most profoundly for aluminum producers are now naturally reluctant to increase capacity. Like everyone else, I trust that this recession ends very quickly and that the expansion of the North American economy, which can so decisively affect our own hopes for the future and the hopes of all less developed countries, will soon be resumed.
It is this situation which to me most vividly illustrates the community of interest and common purpose which should exist between the dollar and sterling areas on the one hand and the less developed countries

on the other. The sustained development of the resources of the less developed countries would not only reduce their economic vulnerability and thus consolidate their vitally important political independence, but at the same time raw materials would continue to be produced for the more advanced industrial nations, thus ensuring the maintenance of high levels of employment and the expansion of world trade, a process which of itself is essential for the survival of the western economies.
In recent years I believe that the common interest and identity of purpose between the wealthier nations and the less developed areas has not been adequately recognized. I hope the forthcoming commonwealth economic conference will give adequate consideration to this basic truth, and in particular pay far greater attention than in the past to the political implications of economic development.
All of us in our separate ways, both as individuals and as nations, desperately seek for a world of peace where men and women may bring up their children in security and with confidence in the future. I believe that apart from general disarmament and the abolition of nuclear tests nothing could do more to achieve this hope than that all like-minded countries should gather together and co-operate in achieving sustained and balanced economic development among themselves, thus expanding world trade and improving the common welfare of all people.
Before I conclude I should like to express the appreciation of my government and the people of Ghana to this great country of Canada for the many manifestations of interest which you have already demonstrated in our affairs since independence, and for the very welcome assistance in a number of fields, economic, social and cultural, which we have received from you. We can best show our appreciation of this assistance by ensuring that it is used for the maximum benefit of all people.
May I thank you once again for the honour and privilege of addressing this great assembly. I pray that this occasion will always be remembered as the beginning of an enduring friendship between Canada and Ghana, a friendship based on a common belief in the dignity of all mankind and in the right of all peoples to control their own affairs, dedicated to the pursuit of peace. Thank you.

speechtext:
It is on behalf of the Canadian Senate, Mr. Prime Minister, that I have the great honour of welcoming you to this house which, in your country as in ours, symbolizes the respect of our two peoples, Ghana and Canada,
Visit of Dr. Nkrumah
for parliamentary democratic institutions, those pillars upon which, notwithstanding differences in culture and tradition, rests the close unity of commonwealth nations.
This union of different peoples under the banner of parliamentary democracy is no mere gesture. The Canadian people which, as you have seen, are made up of various racial communities, have managed, through democratic institutions in their federal form, to fashion and pursue a common ideal and to respect each other's essential characteristics. It is with an equal respect for their diversity and an unshakable faith in their common ideal that Canada looks upon the nations of the commonwealth, whether they be African, like yours, Mr. Prime Minister, Asiatic or Anglo-Saxon.
You are the head of a new African nation, independent within the commonwealth and called to a high destiny, not only on your own continent, but in the whole democratic world as well. Heir to the traditions of ancient Africa's civilization and to British parliamentary institutions and conscious of the responsibility implied by that privilege, your country has already undertaken to give them dynamic and positive expression. Since your recent accession to independence, your government, with astonishing courage, has already started to develop the natural resources of your beautiful country.
Apart from your great love for Africa and your deep understanding of that country, you yourself, Mr. Prime Minister, have brought to your role of nation builder, an extensive knowledge of the North American continent gained during your studies in the United States. It is therefore with very special interest and understanding that Canadians look upon the unfolding of Ghana's destiny. Just as each of the two racial groups who inhabit both our countries are equal partners, enjoying the same rights and privileges, so each and every one of the nations of the commonwealth aTe equal partners jointly and severally pursuing objectives of peace and happiness.
Straight away and by right your country has become a full member of this great and noble commonwealth family. You are welcome into it and, beyond the Atlantic and the African continent, we extend a friendly hand to all the citizens of Ghana whose beloved Sovereign, it seems only fitting to point out, is also ours.
The people of Canada appreciate your having made us this visit in spite of your pressing responsibilities. On my own behalf and on behalf of the Senate of Canada, I ask you to accept our thanks for your kind words and to convey to your compatriots the expression of our sincere admiration and faithful friendship.

maintopic: MEMBERS OF THE SENATE AND OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS CHAMBER, OTTAWA, ON MONDAY, JULY 21, 1958, AT 11 A.M.
speechtext:
Prime Minister Nkrumah, in bringing this memorable session to a conclusion may I add a word of thanks on behalf of the House of Commons. I assure you, sir, that our meeting today has been all too short, having regard to the significance of your visit and the interest you have inspired in us, and in all Canadians, in our brother country of Ghana. We should gladly have given you the unlimited time which is accorded in this chamber to a prime minister or a leader of the opposition, as against the few minutes which you have taken. It would have been a pleasure, too, to hear from the distinguished members of your government who accompany you, and whom we are so happy to welcome. May I express a personal regret that we are not able to meet that remarkable man, Sir Emmanuel Quist, the former Speaker of your legislative assembly, whose contribution to the establishment of parliamentary methods in your new legislature must have been indispensable.
Your visit, in your capacity as representative of the youngest member of the great and growing family of nations which make up the commonwealth, is not only appropriate but it is a touching recognition and furtherance of our fraternal relations. It gives to your older Canadian brother another opportunity to inspect and dote upon the new baby. I hope the metaphor will not be offensive. As Sir Winston Churchill might have said, "Some baby". In fact your phenomenal growth in political stature from the cradle to majority and independence in the last ten years is in contrast to our own unhurried but steady evolution over a century from colony to independence.
From 1791 to 1867 we had three constitutional advances to self-government, and took another 50 years to exercise independence in external affairs. In your case, if we leave out of account the Burns constitution of 1946, which within 18 months was described as outmoded at birth, you rapidly outgrew two new constitutions, those of 1951 and 1954, and reached full stature on March 6, 1957. Then you donned the constitutional garment which you now wear with so much apparent comfort and sophistication.
Apart from this contrast in the rate of our political growth there are many similarities in our history in the commonwealth family. As has been said, we gave the lead to the original four British dominions which, with the United Kingdom, made up the British commonwealth. You have given the lead to the African states. Your democracy, like ours, is modelled on that remarkable British invention of responsible parliamentary government. As I have said on other occasions, this common use of parliamentary institutions which runs throughout the nations of the commonwealth today gives us all an understanding and a confidence in each other's policies and politics which is a solid basis for future friendship and co-operation.
From what I read, you in Ghana have already mastered the parliamentary art. Your great speech in the independence debate, with its understanding of British policy and African needs, its eloquence and its sincerity, its apt quotations from Burke, Aristotle and Tennyson, was in the highest tradition. I am told, too, that if you had any notes on that occasion they were not the copious notes the Speaker hears about in some other houses.
Some other of your new parliamentary practices will endear you to our members. For example, you are reported once to have advised an exasperating member to go have a drink of orange juice. Your ministers, too, seem to follow familiar patterns in dealing with questions before the orders of the day. This example comes from John Gunther:
Mr. Kusi asked the Minister of Agriculture and Natural Resources-
(a)	What is the estimated population of the tsetse fly?
(b)	Is there any evidence that the number is increasing?

speechtext:
(a) There is no available record of tsetse fly population.
(b) In view of the answer to part (a) of the question, the answer is no.
We thank you, sir, for your visit and your message. It has been said that the darkest thing about Africa has been our ignorance of it. You are doing much to dispel this ignorance. We honour you for the outstanding leadership which you are giving in Ghana. We honour your country for its assumption of the responsibilities of self-government. So much depends in West Africa on its success and its example. Please bear with you when you return to Ghana the heartfelt good wishes of the Canadian parliament and people for all your high endeavours.

Tuesday, July 22, 1958
